questions.title: REST Architectural Constraints — What Makes an API Truly RESTful
questions.direct_answer: REST has 6 architectural constraints: client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system, and optional code-on-demand. Most 'REST APIs' are actually HTTP APIs — true REST requires HATEOAS which few implement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know REST is an architectural style, not just HTTP+JSON

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Richardson Maturity Model (Level 0-3) and that most APIs are Level 2 (resources + HTTP verbs), not Level 3 (HATEOAS)

sections.title: Most APIs Claim to Be RESTful — Almost None Actually Are
sections.content:
The most common interview mistake is equating REST with "uses HTTP and returns JSON." REST is an **architectural style defined by six constraints**, and most production APIs satisfy only two or three of them. Roy Fielding's dissertation defines REST as a set of constraints that, when all applied together, produce the scalability and evolvability properties of the web.

The **Richardson Maturity Model** measures how RESTful an API actually is. Level 0 is a single endpoint with POST for everything (RPC over HTTP). Level 1 introduces individual resources with unique URIs. Level 2 adds proper HTTP verbs and status codes — **this is where most production APIs stop.** Level 3 adds HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State), where responses include links to related resources and available actions. Very few APIs reach Level 3 because the client needs to understand hypermedia navigation, which most frontend teams find unnecessary overhead.

Understanding the constraints matters in interviews because it shows you know the difference between "an API that uses HTTP" and "a RESTful API" — and can articulate why most teams deliberately choose Level 2 as the pragmatic sweet spot.

sections.title: The Six REST Constraints — What Each Requires and What Breaks Without It
sections.content:
Each constraint exists to solve a specific distributed systems problem. Knowing the constraint is the easy part — knowing what breaks without it is what interviewers test.

| Constraint | What It Requires | What Breaks Without It |
|---|---|---|
| **Client-Server** | Separate client and server concerns | Tight coupling prevents independent deployment |
| **Stateless** | Each request carries all info needed; no server-side session | Horizontal scaling requires sticky sessions or shared state |
| **Cacheable** | Responses declare cacheability via headers | Every request hits the server; CDNs can't help |
| **Uniform Interface** | Resources identified by URIs, manipulated through representations | Clients need custom logic per endpoint |
| **Layered System** | Client can't tell if it's connected to the origin or intermediary | Proxies, gateways, and load balancers can't be inserted transparently |
| **Code on Demand** (optional) | Server can send executable code (JavaScript) | Not typically used in APIs; the only optional constraint |

**Statelessness is the constraint most APIs violate** without realizing it. If your API requires a server-side session for authentication (storing session ID in memory), you've broken statelessness. JWT tokens solve this by carrying authentication state in the token itself — the server doesn't need to remember anything between requests.

sections.title: Why Level 2 Is the Pragmatic Choice and When HATEOAS Actually Helps
sections.content:
Most teams stop at Level 2 (resources + HTTP verbs + status codes) because the cost of implementing HATEOAS outweighs its benefits for most applications. HATEOAS means every response includes links to related resources and available state transitions — an order response would include links to cancel, pay, or view the associated customer.

**HATEOAS genuinely helps in two scenarios:** APIs consumed by third-party developers who shouldn't hardcode URLs (because you'll change them), and APIs where the available actions depend on resource state (an order can only be cancelled before shipping). For internal APIs with tightly coupled clients, HATEOAS adds serialization overhead and complexity without meaningful benefit.

In interview context, the right answer isn't "HATEOAS is required for REST" or "nobody uses HATEOAS." It's: **"Level 2 REST with proper resources, verbs, and status codes is the industry standard. HATEOAS is valuable when API discoverability matters, but most teams deliberately choose pragmatism over purity."**

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **REST is 6 constraints, not just HTTP + JSON** — statelessness, client-server, uniform interface, layered system, cacheable, and optionally code-on-demand; most APIs calling themselves 'REST' only implement the uniform interface.
- **Statelessness is the hardest constraint to enforce in practice** — every request must carry all state needed to process it; server-side sessions violate statelessness and prevent horizontal scaling.
- **Richardson Maturity Model Level 2 ≠ fully RESTful** — Level 2 (HTTP verbs + resource URIs) is what most APIs implement; Level 3 (HATEOAS) is the actual REST constraint; very few production APIs reach Level 3.
- **Uniform interface = resource-based URIs, not action-based** — `/orders/123/cancel` (action) violates the constraint; `/orders/123` + `PATCH {"status": "cancelled"}` is correct.
- **Cacheability requires `Cache-Control` headers** — `GET` responses without `Cache-Control` are technically non-compliant; explicitly setting `Cache-Control: no-cache` or `max-age` makes cacheable responses explicit.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
REST is not a protocol or a library — it is an architectural style defined by six constraints. The term is widely misused: most APIs described as 'REST APIs' are actually HTTP APIs that partially follow REST principles.

**The constraints that matter in interviews**
- **Stateless** — every request contains all information needed to process it; the server holds no session state; this constraint is what enables horizontal scaling without sticky sessions
- **Uniform interface** — resources identified by URI, manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages, and HATEOAS; the uniform interface is what defines REST, not just using HTTP
- **Layered system** — client cannot tell if it is talking directly to the server or through a proxy, load balancer, or CDN; enables transparent infrastructure changes

**Richardson Maturity Model**
- Level 0: single URI, all operations via POST (SOAP-style)
- Level 1: separate resources (`/orders`, `/customers`)
- Level 2: HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) + correct status codes — this is what most 'REST APIs' actually implement
- Level 3: HATEOAS — responses contain links to related actions; clients discover capabilities rather than hardcoding URIs

Resource-based URIs represent things, not actions: `/orders/123/cancel` is action-based; `/orders/123` with `PATCH {"status": "cancelled"}` is resource-based and the correct pattern.

questions.question: How do you decide which HTTP status code to return? Walk me through the most important ones.
questions.title: HTTP Status Codes — Decision Guide for REST APIs
questions.direct_answer: Use 2xx for success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 4xx for client errors (400 validation, 401 unauthenticated, 403 unauthorized, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 unprocessable), 5xx for server errors (500 internal, 503 unavailable).

interviewer_intent.testing: Correct usage of 401 vs 403, 400 vs 422, 200 vs 204
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 200 for everything including errors, or returning 400 for all validation errors instead of 422
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the semantic distinction between 401 (not authenticated) and 403 (authenticated but not authorized)

sections.title: Status Codes Are Semantic Contracts — Not Just Numbers for Success and Failure
sections.content:
The most common API mistake is returning 200 for everything — including errors wrapped in a JSON body like `{"success": false, "error": "Not found"}`. This breaks HTTP semantics because proxies, caches, and monitoring tools rely on status codes to make decisions. **A CDN caches 200 responses.** If your 200 response contains an error, clients cache the error.

The second most common mistake is confusing **401 (Unauthenticated) with 403 (Unauthorized).** 401 means "I don't know who you are — send credentials." 403 means "I know who you are, and you don't have permission." The response to 401 should include a `WWW-Authenticate` header telling the client how to authenticate. The response to 403 should never include that header — the client is already authenticated.

Another subtle distinction is **400 (Bad Request) vs 422 (Unprocessable Entity).** 400 means the request is syntactically malformed — bad JSON, missing required headers. 422 means the syntax is valid but the content is semantically wrong — trying to create a user with an email that already exists. Most APIs use 400 for both, which is acceptable but less precise.

sections.title: The Status Codes That Matter in Interviews — Grouped by Decision
sections.content:
Instead of memorizing all codes, learn the **decision points** — when you're building an endpoint, these are the choices you actually make.

| Decision | Code | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Success — created something** | 201 Created | POST that created a resource; include `Location` header |
| **Success — no body** | 204 No Content | DELETE or PUT that succeeded with nothing to return |
| **Success — standard** | 200 OK | GET, PUT/PATCH with response body |
| **Client sent bad syntax** | 400 Bad Request | Malformed JSON, missing required fields |
| **Not authenticated** | 401 Unauthorized | No credentials or expired token; include `WWW-Authenticate` |
| **Authenticated but forbidden** | 403 Forbidden | Valid user, insufficient permissions |
| **Resource doesn't exist** | 404 Not Found | ID not found, or hiding 403 for security |
| **Method not allowed** | 405 Method Not Allowed | POST to a read-only resource |
| **Conflict with current state** | 409 Conflict | Duplicate creation, optimistic locking failure |
| **Validation error** | 422 Unprocessable Entity | Valid syntax but semantically wrong data |
| **Rate limited** | 429 Too Many Requests | Include `Retry-After` header |
| **Server error** | 500 Internal Server Error | Unhandled exception — never expose stack traces |

**The `Location` header on 201 is frequently overlooked** — after creating a resource, the response should include `Location: /api/users/42` pointing to the newly created resource.

sections.title: Mapping Your Domain Exceptions to Status Codes — The Spring Pattern That Prevents Drift
Key Points
sections.content:
- **401 vs 403: authentication vs authorization** — `401 Unauthorized` means no valid credentials presented (should authenticate); `403 Forbidden` means credentials are valid but the user lacks permission.
- **`422 Unprocessable Entity` for business rule violations; `400 Bad Request` for malformed input** — a syntactically valid JSON body with an invalid business value is `422`, not `400`.
- **`201 Created` must include a `Location` header** — `Location: /orders/456` tells the client where the new resource lives; returning `200` for a create operation is semantically wrong.
- **`409 Conflict` for optimistic locking failures and duplicate resource creation** — not `400`; the request was well-formed but conflicts with current state.
- **`204 No Content` for successful DELETE and PUT with no response body** — returning `200` with an empty body is ambiguous; `204` explicitly signals 'success, nothing to return'.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HTTP status codes are a contract with API clients. Returning `200` for everything or `400` for all errors forces clients to parse the response body to understand what happened — defeating the purpose of the protocol.

**The decision tree**
- `200 OK` — successful GET, successful PATCH/PUT with response body
- `201 Created` — successful POST that created a resource; must include `Location: /resource/id` header
- `204 No Content` — successful DELETE or PUT with no body to return
- `400 Bad Request` — malformed request syntax, invalid JSON, missing required field that prevents parsing
- `401 Unauthorized` — no credentials provided or credentials invalid; client should authenticate
- `403 Forbidden` — credentials valid, but insufficient permission for this resource or operation
- `404 Not Found` — resource does not exist; also used intentionally to hide existence of restricted resources
- `409 Conflict` — optimistic lock conflict, duplicate key, state machine violation
- `422 Unprocessable Entity` — syntactically valid request, but violates business rules (transfer amount exceeds balance)
- `429 Too Many Requests` — rate limit exceeded; include `Retry-After` header

The `401` vs `403` distinction is the most common interview checkpoint: `401` = 'I don't know who you are'; `403` = 'I know who you are, but no'.

questions.question: What is idempotency in REST APIs? Which HTTP methods are idempotent?
questions.title: Idempotency in REST APIs
questions.direct_answer: An operation is idempotent if calling it multiple times produces the same result as calling it once. GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent. POST is not. PATCH may or may not be, depending on implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand idempotency for retry safety and distributed systems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying DELETE is not idempotent because the second call returns 404 — the resource state is the same (deleted), so it is idempotent
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain idempotency keys for POST operations (Stripe's approach for payment APIs)

sections.title: Idempotency Isn't About the Response Code — It's About the Resource State
sections.content:
The most common interview mistake is saying DELETE is not idempotent because the second call returns 404. **Idempotency is about the final state of the resource, not the response code.** After the first DELETE, the resource is gone. After the second DELETE, the resource is still gone. The server state is identical — that's idempotent.

GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent by specification. **POST is not** — calling POST twice creates two resources. This is why payment APIs use idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key with each POST, and the server returns the same response for duplicate keys instead of processing the request again.

**PATCH is the nuanced case.** A patch that says "set status to ACTIVE" is idempotent — applying it twice produces the same state. A patch that says "increment counter by 1" is not — applying it twice produces a different state. Whether PATCH is idempotent depends entirely on the operation, not the method.

sections.title: HTTP Method Contracts — Safety, Idempotency, and What Infrastructure Assumes
sections.content:
These properties aren't just theoretical — they determine how proxies, load balancers, and API gateways treat your requests. Getting them wrong means infrastructure that was supposed to help you (retry logic, caching) actively works against you.

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Typical Use | Infrastructure Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | ✅ | ✅ | Read resource | Cached by CDN; safe to retry indefinitely |
| HEAD | ✅ | ✅ | Check existence/headers | Same as GET without body |
| PUT | ❌ | ✅ | Replace entire resource | Load balancer may retry on failure |
| DELETE | ❌ | ✅ | Remove resource | Safe to retry — second call returns 404, state is same |
| POST | ❌ | ❌ | Create resource, trigger action | Never cached; never retried automatically |
| PATCH | ❌ | Depends | Partial update | Not retried automatically — idempotency depends on operation |

**The retry column is the practical consequence.** A load balancer that loses the connection after sending a PUT request can safely retry it — sending the same replacement payload twice produces the same final state. A load balancer that loses the connection after sending a POST cannot retry it safely — the operation may have already executed, and retrying would create a duplicate. This is exactly why payment processing APIs use idempotency keys with POST rather than switching to PUT — the semantics of POST (create a new resource) are correct for payments, but the retry problem requires a separate solution.

sections.title: Idempotency Keys — How Stripe Solves the Duplicate Payment Problem
sections.content:
POST endpoints create resources, and network failures make retries dangerous. If a client sends a payment request and the connection drops before receiving the response, the payment may have been processed but the client doesn't know. Retrying could charge the customer twice.

**Idempotency keys** solve this. The client generates a unique key (typically a UUID) and sends it in a header like `Idempotency-Key: abc-123`. The server stores the key with the response. If the same key arrives again, the server returns the stored response without re-executing the logic.

The implementation requires careful decisions: **how long to store keys** (Stripe stores them for 24 hours), **what storage to use** (Redis for distributed systems, database for durability), and **what to do when a key matches but the request body differs** (Stripe returns 422 — the key can't be reused for a different operation). This pattern is essential for any API where duplicate execution has financial or data integrity consequences.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Idempotent ≠ safe** — safe = no side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS); idempotent = same result on repeat (GET, PUT, DELETE, PATCH when absolute); POST is neither safe nor idempotent.
- **DELETE returning `404` on the second call is still idempotent** — idempotency is about server state, not response code; the resource is absent in both cases — that is the consistent outcome.
- **POST with an idempotency key makes it idempotent** — Stripe, PayPal, and AWS use `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` headers; the server stores the first result and returns it for duplicate requests.
- **PATCH is idempotent only if it uses absolute assignment** — `PATCH {"status": "active"}` is idempotent; `PATCH {"count": "+1"}` is not.
- **Retrying non-idempotent operations causes duplicate processing** — network timeouts on POST requests without idempotency keys charge customers twice, create duplicate orders, or send duplicate emails.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Idempotency means calling an operation multiple times has the same effect on server state as calling it once. It is the property that makes safe retries possible — critical for distributed systems where network failures and timeouts are normal.

**Which methods are idempotent by spec**
- GET, HEAD, OPTIONS — safe and idempotent (read-only, no side effects)
- PUT — idempotent: `PUT /orders/123 {"status": "shipped"}` sets the same state every time
- DELETE — idempotent: the resource is absent after the first call; subsequent calls may return `404` but the state (resource absent) is consistent
- POST — not idempotent by default; each call may create a new resource

**Making POST idempotent**
- The client generates a UUID and sends `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` with the request
- The server stores the result keyed by the idempotency key (typically in Redis with a TTL)
- Duplicate requests within the TTL window return the stored result without reprocessing
- Stripe uses this for payment operations — the client can retry safely on timeout without charging the customer twice

A PATCH operation's idempotency depends on the semantics: `{"status": "active"}` is idempotent (absolute assignment); `{"balance": "+10"}` is not (relative change).

questions.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH in REST APIs?
questions.title: PUT vs PATCH — When to Use Each in REST APIs
questions.direct_answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with the payload you send. PATCH applies a partial update to specific fields. PUT is idempotent by definition; PATCH is technically not guaranteed to be idempotent, though most implementations make it so in practice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the semantic difference and can explain the idempotency nuance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using PUT for partial updates — sending only changed fields with PUT technically violates REST semantics because PUT should replace the entire resource.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that PATCH can be idempotent if implemented as absolute field assignments, but is not idempotent for relative operations like incrementing a counter.

sections.title: PUT Replaces the Entire Resource — PATCH Only Changes What You Send
sections.content:
The fundamental difference is **replacement vs modification.** PUT sends a complete representation of the resource — every field must be included. If you omit a field, it should be set to null or its default. PATCH sends only the fields that should change, leaving everything else untouched.

The most common mistake is using PUT for partial updates — sending only changed fields with PUT **technically violates REST semantics** because PUT is defined as a complete replacement. In practice, many APIs accept partial PUT requests, but an interviewer asking this question wants you to know the specification-level distinction.

The practical consequence: **PUT is idempotent by definition** — sending the same complete representation twice produces the same state. PATCH can be idempotent if implemented as absolute field assignments ("set name to Alice"), but is not idempotent if implemented as relative operations ("append 'Jr.' to name"). This makes PUT safer for retries without idempotency keys.

sections.title: PUT vs PATCH — When Each Is the Right Choice
sections.content:
The choice affects idempotency, payload size, and how the server processes the request.

| Aspect | PUT | PATCH |
|---|---|---|
| **Semantics** | Replace the entire resource | Modify specific fields |
| **Payload** | Complete representation (all fields) | Only changed fields |
| **Missing fields** | Set to null/default | Left unchanged |
| **Idempotent** | Always | Depends on operation type |
| **Retry safety** | Safe without idempotency key | May need idempotency key |
| **Bandwidth** | Higher (full resource) | Lower (only changes) |
| **When to use** | Simple resources, replace workflows | Large resources, partial updates |

**In practice, PATCH dominates** for API updates because most updates change one or two fields of a large resource. Requiring the client to send the entire user object just to update an email address wastes bandwidth and creates race conditions — two clients reading the same user, changing different fields, and PUTting back will overwrite each other's changes. PATCH avoids this because each client sends only the field it changed.

sections.title: Why PATCH Is the Safer Default — And the Race Condition PUT Creates With Concurrent Writers
sections.content:
**Use PATCH as your default for update endpoints.** Most updates change one or two fields of a resource that has ten or twenty. Requiring clients to send the complete resource representation for every update creates bandwidth waste, client complexity, and a subtle but serious race condition.

The race condition: Client A reads a user, Client B reads the same user, Client A changes the email and PUTs the full resource, Client B changes the role and PUTs the full resource. Client B's PUT was based on the original state — it includes the old email in its payload. **Client B's update silently overwrites Client A's change.** With PATCH, Client B only sends `{"role": "admin"}` — Client A's email change is preserved.

**Use PUT when the client is replacing an entire resource and you want the idempotency guarantee without an idempotency key.** Configuration objects are a natural fit — replacing a user's notification preferences completely is conceptually a PUT: the client sends the entire new preference set and the old state is discarded. The idempotency guarantee means load balancers can retry without consequence.

For PATCH, the RFC 7396 JSON Merge Patch format is the simplest approach — send a JSON object with only the fields to change, and null to explicitly clear a field. RFC 6902 JSON Patch is more expressive (supports array operations, copy, move) but significantly more complex for clients to construct. Most APIs implement Merge Patch and only reach for JSON Patch when they need fine-grained array manipulation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **PUT = full replacement; PATCH = partial update** — PUT with a partial body technically replaces the resource with the partial representation, nulling out missing fields; PATCH applies only the specified changes.
- **PUT is idempotent; PATCH is idempotent only with absolute assignment** — `PATCH {"status": "active"}` is idempotent; `PATCH {"views": "+1"}` is not.
- **Spring MVC: `@PutMapping` vs `@PatchMapping`** — routing-level distinction; actual idempotency behavior is your implementation's responsibility.
- **JSON Patch (RFC 6902) is the formal PATCH specification** — operations: `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy`, `test`; most APIs implement a simpler 'merge patch' instead.
- **The practical danger of misusing PUT** — a client that does not know about all fields sends `PUT /users/1 {"name": "Alice"}` and wipes `email`, `phone`, and `address` silently; use PATCH for partial updates.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PUT and PATCH both modify resources, but they have fundamentally different semantics that affect how clients must construct requests and how servers must process them.

**PUT — full replacement**
- The request body is the complete new representation of the resource
- Fields missing from the body are treated as null or removed from the resource
- `PUT /users/1 {"name": "Alice"}` — if the server follows PUT semantics strictly, `email` and `phone` are wiped
- Clients must fetch the current state first, modify the fields they want, then PUT the complete object — expensive and racey

**PATCH — partial update**
- Only the fields present in the request body are modified; absent fields are untouched
- More bandwidth-efficient: only send what changed
- Idempotent when using absolute assignment (`"status": "active"`); not idempotent with relative changes (`"count": "+1"`)

**JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch**
- Merge Patch (RFC 7396): simple JSON object, fields present replace existing values, null values delete fields — this is what most APIs implement
- JSON Patch (RFC 6902): array of operation objects (`add`, `remove`, `replace`) — powerful but verbose; used when atomic multi-field operations matter

In practice: use PUT when clients always know the complete state (rare), PATCH for any partial update (most common).

questions.title: REST API Versioning — URI vs Header vs Media Type
questions.direct_answer: URI versioning (/v1/users) is the most pragmatic — visible, cacheable, easy to test. Header versioning (X-API-Version: 2) keeps URLs clean but breaks caching. Media type versioning is REST-pure but complex to implement and test.

sections.title: Three Versioning Strategies — And Why the Industry Can't Agree on One
sections.content:
API versioning seems simple until you realize **there's no industry consensus.** Stripe uses URI versioning (`/v1/charges`), GitHub uses the Accept header (`Accept: application/vnd.github.v3+json`), and some teams use query parameters. Each approach has genuine trade-offs in discoverability, caching, and client complexity.

The interviewer isn't looking for "the right answer" — they want to see you evaluate trade-offs. URI versioning is the most common because it's visible and simple, but it pollutes the URL with version information that isn't part of the resource identity. Header versioning keeps URLs clean but is invisible in browser testing and harder for API consumers to discover.

**The real question behind versioning is deprecation strategy.** How do you migrate clients from v1 to v2? How long do you support old versions? Companies like Stripe solve this with date-based versioning — each API key is pinned to its creation date's version, and changes are additive. This avoids the hard cutover that breaks clients.

sections.title: URI vs Header vs Media Type Versioning — Trade-offs That Matter
sections.content:
Each strategy affects a different part of the API lifecycle.

| Strategy | Example | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **URI path** | `/api/v1/users` | Visible, easy to test in browser, clear routing | Version is not part of resource identity; URL changes break bookmarks |
| **Custom header** | `X-API-Version: 2` | Clean URLs, version independent of resource | Hidden from browsers, easy to forget in clients |
| **Accept header** | `Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json` | Technically most RESTful (content negotiation) | Complex client setup, poor discoverability |
| **Query param** | `/api/users?version=2` | Easy to add, optional | Caching issues — CDNs treat different query params as different resources |

**The pragmatic recommendation:** URI versioning for public APIs where discoverability matters, header versioning for internal APIs where clients are controlled. Stripe's date-based approach (version pinned to API key creation date) is the most client-friendly but requires significant infrastructure investment.

sections.title: Deprecation Strategy — Sunset Headers, Version Pinning, and the Migration Path That Keeps Clients Happy
Key Points
sections.content:
- **URI versioning (`/v1/orders`) is the most discoverable** — visible in browser history, logs, and API gateways; easy to route by prefix; drawback is it violates REST's uniform resource identity (same resource, different URL).
- **Accept header versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json`) is technically correct REST** — the resource URI stays stable; version is a representation negotiation concern; harder to test in browsers.
- **Stripe uses URI versioning; GitHub uses Accept header** — real-world choices are pragmatic, not purely academic; both work at scale.
- **Never remove a version without deprecation notice** — version deprecation requires: announce sunset date in `Sunset` response header, provide migration guide, monitor traffic to the old version before removing.
- **Spring: use `@RequestMapping(path="/v1", headers="API-Version=1")` or router-level versioning** — controller-level annotation versioning creates duplication; prefer API gateway routing or a versioning filter.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
API versioning is how you evolve your API without breaking existing clients. The choice of strategy affects discoverability, REST compliance, and operational complexity.

**Three strategies**
- **URI versioning** (`/api/v1/orders`, `/api/v2/orders`): most common, discoverable, easy to route in API gateways and load balancers; Stripe's model
- **Header versioning** (`API-Version: 2` or custom header): keeps URIs stable; requires custom routing logic; harder to test without tooling
- **Accept/Content-Type versioning** (`Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json`): fully REST-compliant; version is a content negotiation concern; GitHub uses this; complex to implement and consume

**Deprecation — the part most teams get wrong**
- Announce the sunset date in the `Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT` response header on every response from the deprecated version
- Monitor traffic — never remove a version while clients are still calling it; check logs or API gateway metrics
- Provide a concrete migration guide: what changed, what the new endpoint looks like, how to migrate field by field

**In Spring MVC**
- Path prefix versioning is the cleanest: `@RequestMapping("/v1")` on a separate controller class per version
- Copy-paste versioned controllers is an anti-pattern — prefer a shared service layer and version only the request/response DTOs that changed

questions.question: Walk me through the Spring MVC request lifecycle from the moment an HTTP request arrives until a response is returned.
questions.title: Spring MVC Request Lifecycle (DispatcherServlet Flow)
questions.direct_answer: Spring MVC uses a single front controller, DispatcherServlet, which delegates to a chain of specialized components: HandlerMapping finds the controller method, HandlerAdapter invokes it, ViewResolver (or message converters for REST) renders the response, and exception resolvers handle errors along the way.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring MVC internals and ability to reason about what happens at each stage when debugging production issues.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Candidates often jump straight to the controller and skip DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, and HandlerInterceptors, missing three of the most important extension points.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that DispatcherServlet is itself a Servlet registered via web.xml or ServletContainerInitializer, and explain how HandlerInterceptors differ from Filters in terms of Spring context awareness.

sections.title: The DispatcherServlet — One Servlet That Orchestrates the Entire Request Pipeline
sections.content:
Most candidates jump straight to "the request hits the controller." But the controller is step 4 in a pipeline that starts with a single `Servlet` — the **DispatcherServlet.** It's registered by Spring Boot's auto-configuration (or manually via `web.xml` in legacy apps) and acts as a front controller that dispatches every HTTP request to the right handler.

Understanding this pipeline matters because it tells you **where to hook in custom behavior.** Need to log every request? Use a `Filter` — it runs before DispatcherServlet. Need to check authentication before the handler runs? Use a `HandlerInterceptor`.

Need to transform the response after the controller? Use `HandlerInterceptor.afterCompletion`. Each hook point exists at a specific stage. The pipeline is also where Spring's content negotiation, argument resolution, and exception handling happen — none of which are visible if you only think about controllers. Knowing the full lifecycle is what separates candidates who use Spring from those who understand it.

sections.title: Filter Chain → DispatcherServlet — What Runs Before Spring Even Gets Involved
sections.content:
The request first passes through the **Servlet Filter chain.** Filters operate at the Servlet API level — they see the raw `HttpServletRequest` and `HttpServletResponse` before Spring's MVC infrastructure touches them. Security filters (Spring Security's `FilterChainProxy`), CORS filters, and request logging typically happen here.

Filters run in a defined order controlled by `@Order` or `FilterRegistrationBean`. **Each filter can modify the request, modify the response, or short-circuit the chain entirely** — Spring Security's authentication filter returns 401 without ever reaching the DispatcherServlet.

After all filters pass, the DispatcherServlet receives the request. It consults its list of `HandlerMapping` implementations to find which handler (controller method) matches the request URL and HTTP method. `RequestMappingHandlerMapping` is the one that reads `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping`, etc. If no handler matches, DispatcherServlet returns 404.

sections.title: Handler Execution — Argument Resolution, Controller Logic, and Return Value Handling
sections.content:
Once the handler is identified, Spring runs **HandlerInterceptor.preHandle** for all registered interceptors. If any interceptor returns `false`, the request is aborted — the controller never executes. This is the hook point for authentication checks, rate limiting, and request validation that shouldn't live in controller code.

Next, `HandlerAdapter` (specifically `RequestMappingHandlerAdapter`) resolves the controller method's arguments. **`HandlerMethodArgumentResolver`** implementations convert request data into Java objects: `@RequestBody` triggers Jackson deserialization, `@PathVariable` extracts URI template variables, `@RequestParam` reads query parameters, and `@Valid` triggers JSR-303 validation.

The controller method runs, returns a value, and **`HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler`** converts it back to a response. For `@ResponseBody`, this means selecting an `HttpMessageConverter` (typically `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter`) that serializes the return value to JSON. The response body is written, `HandlerInterceptor.postHandle` runs, then `afterCompletion` runs regardless of success or exception.

If the controller throws an exception, `HandlerExceptionResolver` processes it — this is where `@ExceptionHandler` and `@ControllerAdvice` are invoked.

sections.title: Exception Resolution — How @ExceptionHandler Fits Into the Pipeline When Things Go Wrong
sections.content:
When the controller throws an exception, the DispatcherServlet doesn't propagate it to the Servlet container — it first tries to resolve it through the **`HandlerExceptionResolver` chain.** Spring registers several resolvers by default, checked in priority order: `ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver` (handles `@ExceptionHandler` methods), `ResponseStatusExceptionResolver` (handles `@ResponseStatus` annotations on exception classes), and `DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver` (handles Spring MVC's own exceptions like `HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException`).

`ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver` is the one that powers `@ControllerAdvice`. When an exception escapes a controller, this resolver looks for an `@ExceptionHandler` method — first in the current controller class (local scope takes priority), then in all `@ControllerAdvice` beans. It selects the most specific handler: if both `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` and `@ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)` are registered, `ResourceNotFoundException` always picks the more specific handler.

**`afterCompletion` runs regardless of whether an exception was thrown.** This is the cleanup hook — releasing resources, recording metrics, closing traces. It receives the exception as a parameter if one occurred, but it runs even for successful requests. Interceptors should never swallow exceptions in `afterCompletion`; if you catch and log, re-throw or the error disappears silently.

The complete pipeline order for an exception scenario: Controller throws → `HandlerInterceptor.afterCompletion` is queued → `ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver` finds the handler → `@ExceptionHandler` method runs → response is written → `afterCompletion` executes with the original exception. **Understanding this order explains why `@ExceptionHandler` methods in a `@ControllerAdvice` can return structured error responses instead of the Servlet container's default HTML error page** — the resolver intercepts the exception and writes a clean response before it ever reaches Tomcat's error handler.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`DispatcherServlet` is the single entry point for all Spring MVC requests** — it is itself a `javax.servlet.Servlet` registered by `SpringServletContainerInitializer`; the entire MVC pipeline is orchestrated from there.
- **`HandlerMapping` selects the controller method; `HandlerAdapter` invokes it** — `RequestMappingHandlerMapping` maps `@RequestMapping` annotations; `RequestMappingHandlerAdapter` resolves method arguments and invokes the method.
- **`HandlerInterceptor` wraps the controller; `Filter` wraps the entire servlet** — filters execute before `DispatcherServlet`; interceptors execute inside it, after handler resolution.
- **`HttpMessageConverter` reads the request body and writes the response body** — `Jackson2HttpMessageConverter` handles JSON; content negotiation selects the converter based on `Content-Type` and `Accept` headers.
- **`@ExceptionHandler` and `HandlerExceptionResolver` handle exceptions after the handler fails** — `DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver` handles Spring MVC built-in exceptions; `@ControllerAdvice` handles application exceptions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Every HTTP request to a Spring MVC application passes through a fixed pipeline. Knowing each stage is what allows you to place cross-cutting logic in the right layer.

**The pipeline**
- The request hits the servlet container (Tomcat), which forwards it to `DispatcherServlet` — the front controller registered for `/*` or `/`
- `HandlerMapping` resolves which controller method handles this URL + HTTP method combination
- `HandlerInterceptor.preHandle()` runs — authentication checks, logging, rate limiting at the MVC layer
- `HandlerAdapter` invokes the controller method — resolving `@RequestParam`, `@PathVariable`, `@RequestBody` from the request
- `HttpMessageConverter` reads the request body (JSON → Java object) and writes the response body (Java object → JSON)
- `HandlerInterceptor.postHandle()` runs after the handler but before the view is rendered
- The response is written; `HandlerInterceptor.afterCompletion()` runs regardless of success or exception

**Where exceptions go**
- Exceptions thrown by the handler method are caught by `HandlerExceptionResolver`
- `@ExceptionHandler` methods in a `@ControllerAdvice` are picked up by `ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver`

The distinction between `Filter` and `HandlerInterceptor`: a Filter executes before `DispatcherServlet` sees the request — it has no knowledge of which controller will handle it. An interceptor executes inside `DispatcherServlet`, after the handler is resolved.

questions.question: What is the difference between @RestController and @Controller + @ResponseBody in Spring MVC?
questions.title: @RestController vs @Controller + @ResponseBody
questions.direct_answer: @RestController is a composed annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. It marks the class as a Spring component and tells Spring to write every method's return value directly to the HTTP response body via HttpMessageConverter rather than resolving a view name.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Spring's composed annotations and how they affect the response-writing pipeline.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking they are completely interchangeable in all scenarios — @Controller is still needed when a class mixes REST endpoints with view-returning methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how @ResponseBody triggers HttpMessageConverter selection and mention that the same class-level annotation propagates to all methods, so mixing JSON and view responses in one class requires explicit @ResponseBody per method with @Controller.

sections.title: @RestController Is Just @Controller + @ResponseBody — But When You Still Need Plain @Controller
sections.content:
The surface-level answer is simple: `@RestController` combines `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody` into one annotation. Every method in a `@RestController` automatically serializes its return value through an `HttpMessageConverter` (typically Jackson for JSON). With plain `@Controller`, you need `@ResponseBody` on each method that should return data instead of a view name.

**The interview question isn't really about the annotation — it's about `HttpMessageConverter` selection.** When `@ResponseBody` is present, Spring's `RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor` iterates through registered converters and selects the one that matches the response content type. For JSON, that's `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter`. For XML, it's `Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter` (if on classpath). The same mechanism handles `@RequestBody` on the input side.

The case where you still need plain `@Controller` is when a method returns a **view name** — like `"redirect:/login"` or a Thymeleaf template name. `@RestController` would serialize that string as JSON (`"redirect:/login"`) instead of resolving it as a view. In hybrid applications with both API endpoints and server-rendered pages, you need both annotation types on separate controllers.

sections.title: @Controller vs @RestController — What Each Annotation Actually Configures at Runtime
sections.content:
Both annotations register the class as a Spring bean and mark it as a request handler. The difference is entirely in how Spring processes the return value.

| Aspect | @Controller | @RestController |
|---|---|---|
| **Composed of** | @Component + MVC handler detection | @Controller + @ResponseBody |
| **Return value handling** | ViewResolver resolves string as template name | HttpMessageConverter writes directly to response |
| **Method-level override** | Add @ResponseBody per method for JSON output | Add ModelAndView to return a view from one method |
| **Use case** | Server-rendered pages (Thymeleaf, JSP), mixed apps | REST APIs returning JSON or XML |
| **Annotation on class** | @Controller on class applies to all methods | @ResponseBody propagates to all methods |

**The case where you need plain `@Controller` in a modern app:** when a controller serves both API endpoints and redirect/view responses. A login controller might have a GET method that renders the login page (returns a view name) and a POST endpoint for the login API (returns JSON). With `@RestController`, the GET method returns the string `"login"` as JSON — not the Thymeleaf template. With `@Controller`, you annotate only the POST method with `@ResponseBody`.

In practice, most modern Spring Boot applications use `@RestController` everywhere and handle views (if any) in separate dedicated `@Controller` classes. This separation of concerns — REST controllers in one package, view controllers in another — is cleaner than mixing both in a single class.

sections.title: When @ResponseBody Triggers HttpMessageConverter — And How Content Negotiation Selects the Format
sections.content:
When `@ResponseBody` is active, Spring doesn't just blindly serialize to JSON. It runs **content negotiation** to decide the response format. The process checks (in order): the `Accept` header from the client, any `produces` attribute on `@RequestMapping`, and the registered `HttpMessageConverter` list.

If the client sends `Accept: application/xml` and you have the XML converter on the classpath, Spring returns XML — not JSON — even from a `@RestController` method. This surprises developers who assume `@RestController` always means JSON.

**The class-level `produces` attribute controls this explicitly.** `@RestController` combined with `@RequestMapping(produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)` ensures JSON regardless of the `Accept` header. Without it, adding an XML dependency to your classpath can silently change the response format for clients that send `Accept: */*`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody` on every method** — a composed annotation; applying `@ResponseBody` at the class level saves per-method annotation but changes no runtime behavior.
- **`@Controller` is required when returning view names** — returning a `String` from a `@RestController` method writes the string as the response body; in a `@Controller`, it resolves to a view template.
- **`@ResponseBody` triggers `HttpMessageConverter` selection** — the converter chain is walked to find one that supports the return type and the client's `Accept` header; `Jackson2HttpMessageConverter` handles `Object` → JSON.
- **`ResponseEntity<T>` gives full control over status, headers, and body** — `ResponseEntity.created(location).body(dto)` returns `201 Created` with `Location` header without hardcoding the annotation.
- **Content type from `@RequestMapping(produces)` is advisory** — `produces = "application/json"` restricts the mapping to requests accepting JSON but does not prevent `@ResponseBody` from writing XML if an XML converter is also present.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@RestController` is the standard for building REST APIs in Spring. Understanding what the annotation actually does — and why `@Controller` still exists — prevents subtle bugs when views and APIs coexist.

**What the annotations do**
- `@Controller` — marks the class as a Spring MVC handler; return values are interpreted as view names (Thymeleaf/JSP template paths) by default
- `@ResponseBody` — tells Spring to write the return value directly to the HTTP response body via `HttpMessageConverter`, not interpret it as a view name
- `@RestController` — composed annotation that applies both; every method in the class writes its return value to the response body

**When to use `@Controller` instead**
- Server-side rendering with Thymeleaf or JSP — returning a view name that the template engine resolves
- Mixed controllers that serve both HTML pages and REST endpoints — use `@ResponseBody` per method on the REST endpoints

**`ResponseEntity<T>` for full control**
- Return `ResponseEntity.ok(body)` for `200`, `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto)` for `201 Created` with `Location` header, `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()` for `204`
- Use when you need to set custom headers or status codes not expressible with `@ResponseStatus`

questions.question: How do @ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice work together for centralised error handling in Spring MVC?
questions.title: @ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice for Centralised Error Handling
questions.direct_answer: @ExceptionHandler marks a method that handles a specific exception type; when placed inside a @ControllerAdvice class, it applies globally across all controllers in the application, enabling a single, reusable error-handling strategy rather than duplicating catch blocks in every controller.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to design clean, maintainable error handling in a real Spring application rather than scattering try-catch in every controller.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defining @ExceptionHandler only inside a controller class (local scope) when the requirement is global; also returning HTML error pages from a @RestControllerAdvice instead of a structured JSON error body.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the difference between @ControllerAdvice and @RestControllerAdvice, mention that you can scope advice to specific packages or base classes, and show how to map exceptions to RFC 7807 ProblemDetail (Spring 6+).

sections.title: Local @ExceptionHandler Catches One Controller — @ControllerAdvice Catches Them All
sections.content:
The most common mistake is defining `@ExceptionHandler` only inside individual controllers, then wondering why error responses are inconsistent across the API. **A local `@ExceptionHandler` has scope limited to the controller it's defined in.** Move it to a `@ControllerAdvice` class and it handles exceptions from every controller.

The resolution order is important: **local handlers take priority over global ones.** If a controller defines its own `@ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class)` and a `@ControllerAdvice` also handles the same exception, the local one wins. This lets you override global behavior for specific controllers without changing the advice class.

`@RestControllerAdvice` is the REST-friendly variant — it combines `@ControllerAdvice` with `@ResponseBody`, so handler methods automatically serialize their return value to JSON. You can also **scope an advice to specific packages or annotation types** with `@ControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.example.api")` or `@ControllerAdvice(annotations = RestController.class)`. This scoping is valuable in applications that serve both REST APIs and server-rendered pages — different advice classes can return JSON errors for API controllers and HTML error pages for web controllers.

sections.title: Designing the Exception Hierarchy — Business Exceptions, Validation, and the Catch-All
sections.content:
A well-structured error handling strategy has three layers. First, **business exception handlers** for your domain — `ResourceNotFoundException` returns 404, `DuplicateEmailException` returns 409, `InsufficientBalanceException` returns 422. Each maps to a specific HTTP status with a meaningful error message.

Second, a **framework exception handler** for Spring's own exceptions. `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (from `@Valid` failures) should return 400 with a list of field-level errors. `HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException` should return 405 with the allowed methods.

Third, a **catch-all for unexpected exceptions** that returns 500. This is where the catch-all trap matters — never return 400 from a catch-all, or `NullPointerException` becomes "Bad Request" and you'll never notice the bug. Log the full stack trace and return a generic error to the client.

Spring Boot 3.x supports **RFC 7807 ProblemDetail** as a standard response format — `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, and extensible custom fields. Using this standard means all errors follow the same structure without designing a custom schema.

sections.title: RFC 7807 ProblemDetail — The Standard Error Response Body That Clients Can Depend On
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ControllerAdvice` is global; `@RestControllerAdvice` = `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody`** — use `@RestControllerAdvice` so exception handler return values serialize as JSON without additional annotations.
- **Local `@ExceptionHandler` takes precedence over global `@ControllerAdvice`** — when the same exception type is handled both locally and globally, the local handler in the controller wins.
- **Handler method resolution uses the most specific exception type** — `@ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)` wins over `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` when a `ConstraintViolationException` is thrown.
- **`ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` handles Spring MVC internal exceptions** — extend it in your `@ControllerAdvice` and override `handleMethodArgumentNotValid` to customize the `400` response for validation failures.
- **ProblemDetail (RFC 7807, Spring Boot 3.x)** — `ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Order 123 not found")` produces a standardized error body; clients rely on predictable structure instead of parsing free-form messages.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Exception handling in Spring MVC has two levels: local handlers inside a controller, and global handlers in `@ControllerAdvice`. Getting the scoping and precedence right is what determines which handler fires for which exception.

**`@ControllerAdvice` scope**
- By default, applies to all controllers in the application
- Narrow the scope: `@ControllerAdvice(assignableTypes = OrderController.class)` or `@ControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.example.orders")`
- `@RestControllerAdvice` = `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody` — the return value of every `@ExceptionHandler` method is written as the response body via `HttpMessageConverter`

**Handler resolution**
- Spring walks the exception class hierarchy to find the most specific matching `@ExceptionHandler`
- Local handler in the originating controller takes precedence over global `@ControllerAdvice`
- Multiple `@ControllerAdvice` beans: order them with `@Order`; lower value = higher priority

**Extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`**
- Extend it in your `@RestControllerAdvice` to get free handling of Spring MVC built-in exceptions: `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (Bean Validation failures), `NoHandlerFoundException` (404), `HttpMessageNotReadableException` (malformed JSON)
- Override the protected methods to customize the response body format

**ProblemDetail (Spring Boot 3.x)**
- `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` switches Spring's default error responses to RFC 7807 format automatically
- Return `ProblemDetail` from your `@ExceptionHandler` methods for a standardized, interoperable error format

sections.title: Why Validation Belongs in Annotations, Not If-Statements Scattered Through Services
sections.content:
The most common validation mistake is putting validation logic in service methods with manual if-checks — `if (name == null) throw new BadRequest("name required")`. This scatters validation across the codebase, mixes it with business logic, and produces inconsistent error messages.

**Bean validation with `@Valid` separates concerns.** Annotations on the DTO declare what's valid, Spring triggers validation before the controller method runs, and a `@ControllerAdvice` handler formats the error response. The controller never sees invalid data.

The validation pipeline works through `MethodValidationPostProcessor` (for method parameters) and `LocalValidatorFactoryBean` (which wraps Hibernate Validator, the reference implementation). When `@Valid` or `@Validated` is on a parameter, Spring's `HandlerMethodArgumentResolver` triggers validation after deserialization and throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException` if any constraint fails.

**`@Validated` vs `@Valid`:** `@Valid` is JSR-303 standard and supports cascading validation into nested objects. `@Validated` is Spring's extension that adds **validation groups** — separate sets of constraints for create vs update operations. This distinction matters when `id` should be required for updates but absent for creation.

sections.title: Custom ConstraintValidator — When Built-in Annotations Don't Cover Your Rule
Validation Groups and @Validated — Applying Different Constraints for Create vs Update
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Valid` triggers Bean Validation (JSR-380); `@Validated` supports groups** — `@Valid` is Java standard; `@Validated` is Spring's annotation that adds validation group support for staged validation.
- **Validation applies only where you explicitly place the annotation** — `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody` parameter validates the DTO; forgetting `@Valid` means constraints are declared but never evaluated.
- **`ConstraintViolationException` vs `MethodArgumentNotValidException`** — `@RequestBody` + `@Valid` throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException` on failure; `@RequestParam` / `@PathVariable` + `@Validated` throws `ConstraintViolationException`.
- **Cross-field validation requires a class-level `@Constraint`** — annotate the DTO class itself with a custom constraint that receives the entire object; field-level constraints cannot reference sibling fields.
- **`@Valid` on nested objects cascades validation** — an `OrderRequest` containing a `List<LineItem>` validates each `LineItem` only if the list field is annotated `@Valid`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Bean Validation in Spring MVC validates request data before it reaches your service layer, keeping business logic clean and producing consistent `400` responses for invalid input.

**How it wires together**
- Add `@NotBlank`, `@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Pattern` etc. on DTO fields
- Add `@Valid` to the `@RequestBody` parameter in the controller method
- Spring calls the validator before invoking the controller method; on failure it throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`
- Handle in `@ControllerAdvice`: `ex.getBindingResult().getAllErrors()` gives every constraint violation

**Custom constraints**
- Create `@UniqueEmail` annotation + `UniqueEmailValidator implements ConstraintValidator<UniqueEmail, String>`
- `isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx)` — inject a repository and check uniqueness; Spring manages the validator as a bean
- Cross-field validation: annotate the DTO class itself with a class-level constraint that receives the entire object

**`@Valid` vs `@Validated`**
- `@Valid` is the standard Java annotation — use for method parameters in controllers
- `@Validated` is Spring's annotation — enables validation groups (validate different subsets of constraints for create vs update operations)

Cascade validation: a DTO with a nested object field must annotate that field with `@Valid` to propagate validation into the nested object — omitting it silently skips validation of nested constraints.

questions.question: What is the difference between a HandlerInterceptor and a Servlet Filter in Spring MVC, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.title: HandlerInterceptor vs Servlet Filter
questions.direct_answer: A Servlet Filter operates at the Servlet container level and runs before DispatcherServlet, with no access to Spring's context. A HandlerInterceptor runs inside DispatcherServlet's pipeline with full access to the handler (controller method) and ModelAndView, making it the right choice for Spring-specific concerns like authentication, logging with request metadata, or modifying the model before rendering.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring MVC's internal extension points and ability to pick the right tool for cross-cutting concerns.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Implementing everything as Filters because they are more familiar, missing the richer context available to interceptors and the ability to abort after handler resolution.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Filters are better for concerns that must apply to all URLs (including static resources, actuator endpoints) or that need to wrap the request/response stream, such as request body caching for logging.

sections.title: Filters Run Before Spring — Interceptors Run Inside Spring's MVC Pipeline
sections.content:
The core difference is **where in the request pipeline each one operates.** A `Filter` is a Servlet API concept — it runs before `DispatcherServlet`, sees the raw `HttpServletRequest`, and can intercept all URLs including static resources. A `HandlerInterceptor` is a Spring MVC concept — it runs after `HandlerMapping` resolves the controller method and has access to the `handler` object.

This difference determines what each is good for. **Filters are better for concerns that must apply to everything** — CORS headers, request logging, compression, character encoding. Interceptors are better for concerns that **need to know which controller method is about to execute** — checking method-level annotations, measuring handler execution time, or modifying the model.

The common mistake is implementing everything as Filters because they're more familiar from the Servlet spec. But Filters lack Spring MVC context — you can't access the `HandlerMethod`, its annotations, or the `ModelAndView` from a Filter. If your concern needs that context, an interceptor is the right choice.

sections.title: Filter vs HandlerInterceptor — Execution Point and Capabilities
sections.content:
The table maps each concern to the right mechanism based on what information it needs.

| Aspect | Servlet Filter | HandlerInterceptor |
|---|---|---|
| **API level** | Servlet API (`javax.servlet`) | Spring MVC API |
| **Runs when** | Before/after DispatcherServlet | After HandlerMapping, around handler execution |
| **Sees** | Raw request/response | Handler method, annotations, ModelAndView |
| **Static resources** | Yes — intercepts everything | Only matched handler methods |
| **Can wrap request** | Yes (`HttpServletRequestWrapper`) | No |
| **Exception access** | Only through try-catch | `afterCompletion(request, response, handler, ex)` |
| **Use for** | CORS, logging, compression, security | Auth checks on annotations, metrics, model modification |

**The execution order is:** Filters → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → Interceptor.preHandle → Controller → Interceptor.postHandle → View rendering → Interceptor.afterCompletion → Response through Filters. Spring Security's `FilterChainProxy` operates as a Filter, which is why it can reject requests before Spring MVC is involved.

sections.title: Implementing a HandlerInterceptor — The Three Hook Points and What Each Can Access
The Decision Rule — If You Need Handler Metadata or Spring Beans, Use an Interceptor
sections.content:
**Use a Servlet Filter when:** the concern must apply to every URL including static resources, actuator endpoints, and error pages — CORS headers, request logging, compression, character encoding, Spring Security's filter chain. Also use a Filter when you need to wrap the `HttpServletRequest` to cache the body for logging (request body can only be read once without wrapping).

**Use a HandlerInterceptor when:** the concern is Spring MVC-specific — reading method-level annotations, measuring controller execution time, modifying the model before view rendering, or accessing Spring beans that aren't available at Filter registration time. Interceptors are also the right choice when you only want to intercept certain URL patterns and need the mapping logic to be consistent with Spring MVC's own routing.

**The Spring Security answer:** Spring Security uses Filters, not interceptors — by design. Security decisions must happen before Spring MVC processes the request at all, because the controller should never execute if authentication fails. A HandlerInterceptor that rejects a request still invokes the `HandlerMapping` lookup — Spring Security's Filter rejects the request before any Spring MVC infrastructure runs. If you're implementing application-level security (not authentication, but feature-level authorization based on business rules), an interceptor that reads a custom annotation is the right pattern.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Filters execute before `DispatcherServlet`; interceptors execute inside it** — a filter has no access to which controller handled the request; an interceptor does (`Object handler` parameter).
- **Filters apply to all URLs including static resources; interceptors apply only to handler-mapped URLs** — a filter on `/*` also fires for `/static/logo.png`; interceptors skip requests that have no handler mapping.
- **Security, encoding, and CORS belong in filters** — Spring Security is entirely filter-based; CORS handling must intercept the request before `DispatcherServlet` can reject it; character encoding must apply before body parsing.
- **Audit logging and role-based resource checks belong in interceptors** — interceptors receive `HandlerMethod`, allowing access to the controller class and method annotations; filters do not.
- **`HandlerInterceptor.afterCompletion` always runs, even on exception** — suitable for releasing resources, clearing `MDC`, or computing request-level timing regardless of success or failure.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Filters and interceptors both intercept HTTP requests, but they operate at different layers of the stack. The choice determines what context you have access to and what requests you can affect.

**Filters (Servlet layer)**
- Part of the Servlet spec; execute in a chain before `DispatcherServlet`
- Access to raw `HttpServletRequest` and `HttpServletResponse` only — no Spring context
- Apply to every request matching the URL pattern, including static resources
- Use for: authentication (Spring Security), encoding (`CharacterEncodingFilter`), CORS, request/response logging at the raw HTTP level

**HandlerInterceptors (Spring MVC layer)**
- Registered with Spring MVC's `HandlerMapping`; execute inside `DispatcherServlet` after handler resolution
- `preHandle(request, response, handler)` receives the resolved `HandlerMethod` — inspect controller annotations, method names, class types
- Only fire for requests that map to a handler — static resources and 404s do not trigger interceptors
- Use for: audit logging with handler context, `@RequiresPermission` annotation checks, user locale/timezone setup

**`afterCompletion` is the cleanup hook**
- Fires after the response is committed, even when an exception was thrown
- Correct place to remove `MDC` entries, release thread-local resources, or record timing metrics

sections.title: OFFSET 10000 Scans 10,000 Rows Before Returning Anything — Why Offset Pagination Breaks at Scale
sections.content:
Most developers implement pagination with `OFFSET` and `LIMIT` because it maps directly to page numbers — page 5 with 20 items is `OFFSET 80 LIMIT 20`. The problem is performance. **The database must scan and discard all rows before the offset** to find your page. `OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20` reads 10,020 rows and throws away 10,000. At page 500 of a million-row table, the query takes seconds.

Cursor-based pagination solves this by using a **pointer to the last item seen** instead of a numeric offset. The query becomes `WHERE id > :lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20` — the database uses an index seek and reads exactly 20 rows regardless of how deep into the dataset you are.

This is why **Stripe, GitHub, and Twitter all use cursor-based pagination** for their high-volume APIs. The trade-off is that cursor pagination doesn't support jumping to arbitrary pages — you can only go forward or backward from the current position. For most API use cases (infinite scroll, feed navigation), this is perfectly fine.

sections.title: Offset vs Cursor Pagination — Performance, Flexibility, and When Each Fits
sections.content:
The choice depends on whether your users need page numbers or just forward/backward navigation.

| Aspect | Offset-Based | Cursor-Based |
|---|---|---|
| **Query pattern** | `OFFSET n LIMIT m` | `WHERE id > :cursor LIMIT m` |
| **Performance at depth** | Degrades linearly — scans all skipped rows | Constant — index seek to cursor |
| **Random page access** | Yes — page 50, page 200 | No — forward/backward only |
| **Data consistency** | Rows shift when inserts/deletes happen between pages | Stable — cursor anchors to a specific row |
| **URL** | `?page=5&size=20` | `?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ&size=20` |
| **Best for** | Admin dashboards, small datasets | Public APIs, feeds, large datasets |

**The consistency issue is subtle but important.** With offset pagination, if a new row is inserted on page 1 while you're reading page 2, every row shifts forward — you either see a duplicate or miss a row. Cursor pagination anchors to a specific row, so inserts and deletes elsewhere don't affect your result.

sections.title: Implementing Cursor Pagination in Spring Data — The Keyset Pattern
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`OFFSET n` scans and discards n rows** — `OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20` scans 10,020 rows; performance degrades linearly with page depth; unacceptable for large datasets.
- **Cursor pagination uses a stable `WHERE id > :lastId` clause** — one index seek regardless of page depth; constant-time regardless of how deep into the result set you go.
- **Offset pagination allows random page access; cursor does not** — offset supports 'jump to page 47'; cursor requires sequential traversal; the right choice depends on the UI pattern.
- **Spring Data: `Pageable` + `Page<T>` runs two queries** — one for data, one `COUNT(*)` for total pages; `Slice<T>` fetches only data + one more row (to detect `hasNext`); prefer `Slice` when total count is unnecessary.
- **Cursor must be stable and unique** — using `created_at` alone as cursor breaks on rows with identical timestamps; use `(created_at, id)` composite cursor for strict ordering.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Pagination is a ubiquitous feature with a hidden performance trap. Offset-based pagination works fine on small datasets and breaks catastrophically on large ones.

**Why offset breaks at scale**
- `SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at OFFSET 50000 LIMIT 20` — the database sorts and discards 50,000 rows to return 20
- Performance degrades linearly with page depth; page 2,500 is 2,500× slower than page 1
- Facebook, Twitter, Instagram all migrated away from offset for their feeds

**Cursor pagination**
- `WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`
- One index seek; constant time regardless of page depth
- Trade-off: no random access — you cannot jump to page 47; must traverse sequentially
- Cursor must be stable and unique — use a composite `(created_at, id)` cursor; timestamp alone breaks on ties

**Spring Data choices**
- `Page<T>` — runs two SQL queries: data query + `COUNT(*)`; use when the UI shows total page count
- `Slice<T>` — fetches `limit + 1` rows to detect `hasNext`; no COUNT query; use for 'load more' UIs

The decision rule: offset for admin UIs with small data and random page access; cursor for feeds, timelines, and any pagination over more than ~10,000 rows.

sections.title: CORS Blocks Legitimate Requests When Configured at the Wrong Level — Or Duplicated Across Levels
sections.content:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the browser's mechanism for controlling which origins can call your API. The most common configuration mistake isn't forgetting CORS — it's **configuring it at multiple levels simultaneously.** Adding CORS headers manually in a Filter while also configuring them via Spring MVC's `CorsRegistry` causes duplicate headers that some browsers reject entirely.

Spring provides CORS configuration at three levels: **annotation-level** (`@CrossOrigin` on controllers or methods), **global MVC-level** (via `WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings`), and **filter-level** (`CorsFilter` bean). Each level applies at a different point in the request pipeline, and using more than one for the same endpoint produces duplicate `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers.

The critical distinction interviewers test is between **simple requests and preflight requests.** Simple requests (GET, POST with standard content types) go straight through. Non-simple requests (PUT, DELETE, custom headers, JSON content type) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request — the browser asks permission before sending the actual request. If your CORS config doesn't handle OPTIONS, the preflight fails and the actual request never fires.

sections.title: Three Configuration Levels — When to Use Each and Why Mixing Them Breaks
Spring Security and CORS — Why the Security Chain Must Know About Your CORS Config
Key Points
sections.content:
- **CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server** — the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`; the browser decides whether to allow the JavaScript to read the response; backend-to-backend calls are unaffected.
- **Preflight requests are HTTP OPTIONS** — browsers send `OPTIONS` before non-simple cross-origin requests; the server must respond with the allowed methods/headers; a missing handler causes CORS failures that look like network errors.
- **`@CrossOrigin` on the controller and `CorsRegistry` in `WebMvcConfigurer` are additive** — if both are configured for the same endpoint with different origins, both sets are merged; ensure they are consistent.
- **Spring Security's CORS support must be enabled explicitly** — if Spring Security is present, configure CORS through `http.cors()` pointing to the same `CorsConfigurationSource`; configuring only `WebMvcConfigurer` bypasses the filter chain.
- **`allowedOrigins("*")` conflicts with `allowCredentials(true)`** — cookies and credentials require an explicit origin, not a wildcard; `allowedOriginPatterns("https://*.example.com")` allows patterns with credentials.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
CORS is a browser security mechanism that restricts JavaScript from reading responses from a different origin. Understanding CORS means understanding that the browser is the enforcer — the server only sends headers.

**How a cross-origin request works**
- Simple requests (GET, POST with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`): browser sends the request, then checks if the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header permits the origin
- Preflight: browser sends `OPTIONS` first; server must respond with permitted methods, headers, and origins; then the actual request is sent

**Configuration in Spring MVC**
- `@CrossOrigin(origins = "https://app.example.com")` on a controller or method — fine-grained, easy to understand
- `WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings()` — global configuration for all or specific path patterns
- Both can coexist — they are merged, not overridden

**Spring Security interaction**
- Spring Security's filter chain processes requests before `DispatcherServlet`; if Security rejects the preflight OPTIONS request, it never reaches the MVC CORS configuration
- Configure CORS via `http.cors(cors -> cors.configurationSource(corsConfigSource))` so it applies at the filter chain level

**The wildcard + credentials trap**
- `allowedOrigins("*")` with `allowCredentials(true)` is rejected by the browser spec
- Use `allowedOriginPatterns("https://*.example.com")` to allow subdomains with credentials
