sections.title: CSRF Protection on a Stateless JWT API Is Overhead Without Benefit — But Cookie-Based Auth Needs It
sections.content:
The most common security mistake in REST APIs is applying the wrong protection for the authentication model. **CSRF protection exists to prevent forged requests from authenticated browser sessions** — the browser automatically attaches cookies, so a malicious site can trigger requests that the server thinks are legitimate. If your API uses JWT tokens in the `Authorization` header, CSRF is irrelevant — headers are never sent automatically by the browser.

But if your API uses **cookie-based session authentication** (which Spring Security does by default), CSRF protection is essential. Disabling it because "we're building a REST API" is a security vulnerability when the API is called from a browser with session cookies.

The modern alternative is the **`SameSite` cookie attribute.** Setting `SameSite=Lax` or `SameSite=Strict` prevents the browser from sending cookies on cross-site requests, which is exactly what CSRF tokens protect against. `SameSite=Lax` allows cookies on top-level navigation (following links) but blocks them on cross-site form submissions and AJAX — covering the most common CSRF attack vectors without token management overhead.

sections.title: Configuring Spring Security for Stateless REST APIs — What to Disable and What to Add
sections.content:
For a typical JWT-based REST API, the Spring Security configuration disables unnecessary features and adds the appropriate ones. The choices aren't arbitrary — each line reflects a deliberate decision about the authentication model.

```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain apiSecurity(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())  // No cookies = no CSRF risk
        .sessionManagement(sm -> sm.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS))
        .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())  // Enable CORS with WebMvcConfigurer config
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .build();
}
```

**`sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS)` is critical** — it tells Spring Security to never create an `HttpSession`. Without this, Spring creates sessions on every request even with JWT authentication, wasting memory and breaking horizontal scaling. Each server instance would maintain its own session store, and requests routed to a different instance would fail authentication.

CORS must be configured via `cors(Customizer.withDefaults())` **and** a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean. Spring Security delegates to the registered `CorsConfigurationSource` — if you skip the `cors()` call here, Spring Security's filter chain rejects preflight OPTIONS requests with 403 before they reach the MVC CORS handler. The two configurations must both be present: this line to enable the delegation, and the separate bean to define the allowed origins and methods.

sections.title: When Cookie Auth Still Needs CSRF — And How the SameSite Attribute Changes the Calculus
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Disable CSRF for stateless JWT APIs — it only protects session-cookie auth** — CSRF exploits the browser automatically sending session cookies; JWTs in `Authorization` headers are not sent by browsers automatically, so the attack vector does not exist.
- **Enable CSRF for session-cookie-based apps** — Spring Security uses the Synchronizer Token Pattern: a hidden form field or header must match a server-side token; forged requests from other origins cannot include it.
- **`SameSite=Strict` on session cookies is a modern CSRF mitigation** — browsers refuse to send the cookie on cross-origin requests; no need for CSRF tokens; supported by all modern browsers.
- **CORS headers do not protect your API from server-side attackers** — CORS is a browser mechanism; a curl request from a server ignores CORS entirely; backend-to-backend calls are unaffected by CORS configuration.
- **CSRF token in header (`X-XSRF-TOKEN`) suits SPAs** — Spring Security's `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` writes the token to a readable cookie; the SPA reads and sends it as a header on every mutating request.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
CORS and CSRF are two separate security concerns that are commonly confused because both involve cross-origin requests. They protect against different attacks and are configured independently.

**CORS — protecting the browser from reading unauthorized responses**
- The browser checks `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to decide if JavaScript can read the response
- CORS does not prevent the request from reaching the server — it prevents the response from being readable by the origin JavaScript
- Backend-to-backend calls ignore CORS entirely — only browser-originated JavaScript is affected

**CSRF — protecting session-cookie apps from forged requests**
- The attack: malicious site tricks the user's browser into sending a request to your API; browser automatically includes the session cookie
- The fix: require a secret token that the malicious site cannot access (Synchronizer Token Pattern)
- For SPAs: `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` writes the CSRF token to a JavaScript-readable cookie; the SPA reads it and sends it as `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header

**When to disable CSRF**
- Stateless JWT APIs: the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header is not sent automatically by browsers; the cross-site forgery attack vector does not apply
- `http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())` in your Spring Security configuration

Modern apps using `SameSite=Strict` cookies get CSRF protection for free from the browser — the cookie is never sent on cross-origin requests.

sections.title: Why HashMap-Based Rate Limiting Crashes Under Load and What Algorithms Actually Work
sections.content:
The quickest way to implement rate limiting — a `HashMap<String, AtomicInteger>` tracking request counts per IP — has two fatal flaws. **It's not thread-safe** across concurrent requests (race conditions on increment and check), and it's not distributed (each server instance has its own counter, so users get N times the rate limit across N servers).

Production rate limiting requires two decisions: **which algorithm** to use and **where to store the state.** The algorithm determines fairness and burst behavior. The storage determines whether it works in a distributed deployment.

The three main algorithms are **fixed window** (count requests in calendar-aligned intervals — simple but allows 2x burst at window boundaries), **sliding window** (smooths the boundary burst by weighting the previous window's count), and **token bucket** (accumulate tokens at a fixed rate, spend one per request — allows controlled bursts and is the most commonly used in production). Redis is the standard state store because it provides atomic operations, TTL-based key expiry, and shared state across all server instances.

sections.title: Rate Limiting Algorithms — Fixed Window vs Sliding Window vs Token Bucket
sections.content:
The algorithm determines how burst traffic is handled. Each has a different failure mode, and the right choice depends on whether you're protecting against sustained abuse or accidental spikes.

| Algorithm | How It Works | Burst Behavior | Weakness | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed Window** | Count requests in calendar-aligned intervals (e.g., 100/minute) | Allows 2× burst at window boundary | Two bursts back-to-back span the boundary — client gets 200 requests in 2 seconds | Simple use cases, internal APIs |
| **Sliding Window Log** | Track timestamp of each request; count last N seconds exactly | Smooth, no boundary burst | High memory — store every request timestamp | Premium APIs, exact accuracy needed |
| **Sliding Window Counter** | Weighted average of current + previous window counts | Near-smooth approximation | Slightly imprecise at boundaries | Most production APIs — good balance |
| **Token Bucket** | Accumulate tokens at fixed rate; spend one per request | Allows controlled bursts up to bucket capacity | Complexity — must track both tokens and refill time | APIs with legitimate burst patterns |
| **Leaky Bucket** | Queue requests; process at fixed rate; reject overflow | No burst — steady output regardless of input | Adds latency; queue management overhead | Traffic shaping, webhook delivery |

**Token bucket is the production standard** because it models natural traffic patterns accurately. A mobile client making API calls as a user taps through screens produces natural bursts — several requests in quick succession, then silence. Token bucket allows these bursts (up to the bucket capacity) while enforcing the sustained rate limit. Fixed window would penalize the user for a legitimate burst of activity that happens to cluster at the window boundary.

The choice between in-memory and Redis-backed storage is determined by your deployment: single-instance apps can use in-memory (Bucket4j's in-memory implementation), multi-instance deployments need Redis to share counter state across all nodes.

sections.title: Token Bucket with Redis — The Production-Standard Implementation
sections.content:
The token bucket algorithm maintains a bucket that fills with tokens at a fixed rate. Each request consumes one token. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. Bursts are naturally handled — a user who hasn't made requests for a while has a full bucket.

**Spring Cloud Gateway includes a built-in Redis rate limiter** using token bucket. For Spring MVC APIs, implement it as a `HandlerInterceptor` or Servlet Filter backed by Redis.

The key Redis operations must be **atomic** — check the current token count, decrement it, and set the TTL in a single Lua script. Separate GET-and-SET operations create race conditions where two concurrent requests both see 1 remaining token and both proceed.

Always return the **standard rate limit headers** in every response: `X-RateLimit-Limit` (max requests), `X-RateLimit-Remaining` (tokens left), `X-RateLimit-Reset` (when the bucket refills). When rejecting a request, return `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header. These headers let well-behaved clients self-throttle instead of hammering the API and getting rejected.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **In-memory rate limiting breaks in multi-instance deployments** — `ConcurrentHashMap` state is local to each instance; a client that hits different instances can bypass the limit by the factor of instance count.
- **Redis + sliding window is the production-standard approach** — atomic Lua scripts or Redis sorted sets track request timestamps per client; state is shared across all instances.
- **Token bucket vs fixed window vs sliding window** — fixed window allows 2× the limit at window boundaries; sliding window prevents bursting; token bucket allows controlled bursting up to the bucket size.
- **`429 Too Many Requests` + `Retry-After` header** — inform the client how long to wait; avoid exponential backoff hammering by all clients simultaneously (add jitter).
- **Rate limit by client identity, not just IP** — behind a NAT or proxy, many users share one IP; use API key, JWT subject, or authenticated user ID as the rate limit key.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Rate limiting protects your API from being overwhelmed by a single client — whether through abuse, misconfigured retry logic, or denial-of-service. The implementation strategy matters significantly for distributed deployments.

**Why in-memory rate limiting fails in production**
- Each application instance maintains its own counter
- A client making 100 requests per minute across 5 instances can make 500 total without triggering any single instance's limit
- In-memory works only for single-instance deployments or as a local pre-check before a distributed check

**Algorithms**
- **Fixed window**: count requests per time window (e.g., per minute); simple but allows 2× the limit at window boundaries (end of old window + start of new)
- **Sliding window**: track individual request timestamps; accurate but memory-intensive
- **Token bucket**: a bucket of tokens refills at a fixed rate; clients consume tokens; allows controlled bursting up to the bucket capacity

**Redis-based implementation**
- Use an atomic Lua script or Redis `ZADD`/`ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` on a sorted set keyed by `clientId:minute`
- Bucket4j and Resilience4j both support Redis-backed rate limiting with Spring Boot integration

**Response**
- Return `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 60` header
- Rate limit key should be authenticated user ID or API key — never just IP address behind shared NAT

questions.question: How do DeferredResult and CompletableFuture enable asynchronous request processing in Spring MVC controllers?
questions.title: Async Controllers with DeferredResult and CompletableFuture
questions.direct_answer: Returning DeferredResult or CompletableFuture from a controller method releases the Servlet container thread immediately while the response is held open. The result is set asynchronously from another thread (a pool, a callback, or a reactive pipeline), allowing the container to handle more concurrent requests without blocking threads on I/O-bound work.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of thread management in web servers and how async Servlet support translates to scalability improvements.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking that returning CompletableFuture automatically makes the underlying operation non-blocking — if the CompletableFuture wraps a blocking JDBC call, the thread is still blocked, just a different thread.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Servlet 3.0 async model that underlies both mechanisms, mention timeout configuration, error handling via DeferredResult.setErrorResult or CompletableFuture exceptionally, and when to prefer Spring WebFlux instead.

sections.title: Returning CompletableFuture Doesn't Make Your Code Non-Blocking — It Frees the Servlet Thread
sections.content:
The biggest misconception about async controllers is that returning `CompletableFuture` or `DeferredResult` makes the underlying operation non-blocking. **It doesn't.** If your `CompletableFuture` wraps a blocking JDBC call, that call still blocks — it just blocks a different thread instead of the servlet thread.

The actual benefit is **servlet thread release.** In a traditional synchronous controller, the servlet container's thread pool (typically 200 threads in Tomcat) holds one thread per request until the response is complete. A slow database query holds a servlet thread for its entire duration. With async, the servlet thread is released immediately after dispatching the work, freeing it to handle other requests.

This matters when you have **high concurrency with slow downstream calls.** If your API calls an external service that takes 2 seconds to respond, synchronous processing handles at most 200 concurrent requests (one per thread). Async processing lets the 200 servlet threads cycle through thousands of requests while the downstream calls complete on a separate executor.

sections.title: DeferredResult vs CompletableFuture — When You Control the Completion vs When You Chain It
sections.content:
`CompletableFuture<ResponseEntity<T>>` as a return type is the simpler approach — Spring detects the async type, starts Servlet 3.0 async processing, and completes the response when the future resolves. Use it when the async operation is a single call that returns a result.

`DeferredResult<ResponseEntity<T>>` gives you **explicit control over completion.** You hold a reference to the `DeferredResult`, and any thread — an event listener, a message consumer, a scheduled task — can call `setResult()` or `setErrorResult()` later. This makes `DeferredResult` the right choice for long-polling, event-driven responses, or cases where completion is triggered by an external event.

**Timeout configuration is critical for both.** Without a timeout, an async request that never completes holds server resources indefinitely. Set `spring.mvc.async.request-timeout=30000` globally, or call `deferredResult.setTimeout(30000L)` per request. When the timeout fires, Spring calls the timeout callback (if registered) or returns 503 Service Unavailable.

sections.title: DeferredResult vs CompletableFuture — Completion Control and What Each Is Good For
sections.content:
Both types signal Spring to use Servlet 3.0 async processing, but they differ in who controls completion and how the result is set.

| Aspect | DeferredResult | CompletableFuture |
|---|---|---|
| **Completion model** | Explicit — any thread calls `setResult()` | Functional — chains via `thenApply()`, `thenCompose()` |
| **Error handling** | `setErrorResult(exception)` | `exceptionally()` or `handle()` in the chain |
| **Timeout handling** | `setTimeout()` + `onTimeout()` callback | `spring.mvc.async.request-timeout` property |
| **Cancellation** | `onCompletion()` callback when client disconnects | No built-in cancellation signal |
| **Best for** | Long-polling, event-driven responses, callback-based APIs | Async service calls, parallel operations, reactive bridging |
| **Thread model** | Completion thread sets result; any thread works | Configured executor or ForkJoinPool |

**`DeferredResult` is the right choice for long-polling.** Imagine a notification endpoint where the client holds the connection open waiting for an event. The controller stores the `DeferredResult` in a map keyed by user ID. When an event arrives (from a message queue consumer, a WebSocket, anything), the event handler retrieves the stored `DeferredResult` and calls `setResult()` — the client receives the response immediately without polling. `onCompletion()` cleans up the map entry when the client disconnects.

**`CompletableFuture` is the right choice** when you're composing results from multiple async service calls — `CompletableFuture.allOf(serviceA.call(), serviceB.call())` runs them in parallel and completes when both finish. The key reminder: wrap the result in a `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> blockingCall(), executor)` to run on the executor's thread pool — if you run it on the calling thread, you block the Servlet thread and gain nothing.

sections.title: When Async MVC Reaches Its Limit — The Cases That Actually Call for Spring WebFlux
sections.content:
Async Spring MVC frees Servlet threads but doesn't eliminate blocking. If your `CompletableFuture` wraps a JDBC call, that call blocks a thread from a different pool — you've shifted the bottleneck, not removed it. The total thread count across all pools is still proportional to concurrent requests.

**Spring WebFlux genuinely eliminates blocking** by building on a non-blocking I/O event loop (Netty) with a reactive programming model (Project Reactor). With WebFlux, a single event loop thread handles thousands of concurrent requests — the thread is never blocked waiting for I/O. The catch: your entire call stack must be non-blocking. Mixing reactive code with blocking JDBC calls eliminates the benefit.

**Choose async Spring MVC when:** you're adding async to an existing Spring MVC application, your team isn't familiar with reactive programming, you have a few high-latency endpoints that need async behavior mixed with many synchronous endpoints, or your downstream systems don't offer reactive drivers.

**Choose Spring WebFlux when:** you're building a new service from scratch, your team understands reactive programming, you're integrating with WebClient (non-blocking HTTP), R2DBC (non-blocking JDBC), or Reactive MongoDB, and you need to handle a very high number of concurrent long-lived connections (streaming, SSE, WebSocket).

The practical heuristic: **if you're wrapping blocking calls in `CompletableFuture`, async MVC gives you marginal benefit and real complexity.** Consider whether the simpler synchronous model with a larger thread pool achieves the same throughput at lower operational complexity.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Async controllers free the Tomcat thread; the operation itself may still be blocking** — returning `CompletableFuture` releases the HTTP worker thread but if the future runs `JDBC` calls synchronously, you have just moved the blocking to a different thread pool.
- **`DeferredResult` is manually completed; `CompletableFuture` is completion-stage-based** — `DeferredResult.setResult()` is called explicitly from any thread; `CompletableFuture` integrates with `thenApply`, `thenCompose` chains.
- **`@Async` + `CompletableFuture` return type is the Spring-idiomatic pattern** — annotate the service method with `@Async`; the controller returns the future; Spring completes it on the async thread pool.
- **Timeout handling is mandatory** — `DeferredResult(timeout)` sets a max wait time; uncompleted results after timeout fire the timeout handler; `CompletableFuture.orTimeout()` on Java 9+ applies the same pattern.
- **True non-blocking requires WebFlux + Reactor** — `CompletableFuture` in Spring MVC is better concurrency than synchronous blocking, but WebFlux with `Mono`/`Flux` is fully non-blocking at the I/O layer.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Async controllers in Spring MVC release the Tomcat thread pool thread while waiting for a long operation to complete. This improves throughput for I/O-bound workloads — but it does not make blocking operations non-blocking.

**`CompletableFuture<T>` return type**
- Return `CompletableFuture<ResponseEntity<T>>` from the controller method
- Tomcat thread is released immediately after returning the future; Servlet 3.0 async support keeps the connection open
- When the future completes, Spring writes the response
- Combine with `@Async` on the service method: the service runs on the async thread pool; the controller returns the future without blocking

**`DeferredResult<T>`**
- Create `DeferredResult<T>` in the controller and return it — Tomcat thread is released
- Store the `DeferredResult` reference; call `deferredResult.setResult(value)` from any thread when the operation completes
- Use when the completion signal comes from an external event (message received, WebSocket frame, internal cache update)

**The critical misconception**
- Async controller = fewer Tomcat threads occupied
- The underlying operation (database query, HTTP call) may still block a thread in a different pool
- True end-to-end non-blocking requires WebFlux + reactive database drivers + reactive HTTP clients

questions.title: OpenAPI Documentation with SpringDoc
questions.direct_answer: Use springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui to auto-generate OpenAPI 3 spec from your code. Enrich with @Operation, @ApiResponse, and @Schema annotations. Expose the UI at /swagger-ui.html.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to document APIs for other teams

sections.title: springfox Is Dead — springdoc-openapi Is the Only Maintained Option
sections.content:
The first thing to get right is the library choice. **springfox (Swagger 2) has been abandoned** — the last release was 2020, it doesn't support Spring Boot 3.x, and it generates Swagger 2.0 specs instead of the current OpenAPI 3.0 standard. Most online tutorials still reference springfox, which trips up developers who follow them.

**springdoc-openapi** is the active, maintained library. Add `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui` to your Spring Boot 3.x project, and it auto-generates an OpenAPI 3.0 spec from your controllers, models, and annotations. The Swagger UI is available at `/swagger-ui.html` and the raw spec at `/v3/api-docs` — no additional configuration needed for basic usage.

Beyond documentation, OpenAPI specs enable **contract-first development and code generation.** Write the spec first, generate server stubs and client SDKs from it. This prevents documentation drift — the spec is the source of truth, not an afterthought generated from annotations.

**Zero-config setup with springdoc:** adding a single dependency — `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui` — is all that's needed for basic documentation. The Swagger UI auto-appears at `/swagger-ui.html` and the raw OpenAPI 3 JSON spec at `/v3/api-docs`. springdoc scans all `@RestController` classes at startup, reads method signatures and annotations, and generates the spec. Models are inferred from parameter types and return types — no separate schema registration. The generated spec works immediately with Postman, curl, and any OpenAPI-compatible tooling, even before you add a single documentation annotation.

sections.title: Enriching Generated Documentation — Annotations That Make the Spec Useful
JWT Authentication in Swagger UI — Making Security Work During API Testing
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Springfox is deprecated — use Springdoc** — `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui` generates OpenAPI 3.x documentation; Springfox has not been updated since 2020 and conflicts with Spring Boot 3.x.
- **OpenAPI spec enables contract-first development** — generate the spec first; use `openapi-generator` to generate client SDKs in Java, TypeScript, Python from the same spec.
- **`@Operation`, `@ApiResponse`, `@Schema` are optional enhancements** — Springdoc reads `@RequestBody`, `@RequestParam`, `@PathVariable`, and return types automatically; annotations add descriptions and examples.
- **Secure endpoints in Swagger UI with security scheme configuration** — `@SecurityScheme` + `@SecurityRequirement` adds the `Authorize` button; developers can test JWT-protected endpoints without Postman.
- **Hide internal or sensitive endpoints with `@Hidden`** — exclude endpoints from the generated spec; useful for actuator endpoints or internal admin APIs that should not be in the public documentation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Springdoc generates OpenAPI 3.x documentation from your Spring MVC controllers automatically — no XML, no separate doc server. The generated spec is the contract that clients, tests, and SDK generators consume.

**Setup**
- Add `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui` dependency
- Swagger UI is available at `/swagger-ui.html`; the raw OpenAPI JSON/YAML at `/v3/api-docs`
- Springdoc introspects `@RequestMapping`, `@RequestBody`, `@PathVariable`, return types — zero additional annotations needed for basic documentation

**Enriching the documentation**
- `@Operation(summary = "Create order", description = "...")` — describes the endpoint
- `@ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = "Order created")` — documents response codes
- `@Schema(description = "ISO 4217 currency code", example = "USD")` — documents DTO fields with examples

**Securing Swagger UI**
- Configure `@SecurityScheme(type = SecuritySchemeType.HTTP, scheme = "bearer")` on a configuration class
- Annotate secured endpoints with `@SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth")`
- Developers click 'Authorize', enter a JWT, and test protected endpoints directly from the UI

Export the spec at `/v3/api-docs.yaml` and use `openapi-generator-cli` to produce type-safe client libraries — one source of truth for the API contract shared between backend and frontend teams.

questions.question: How does content negotiation work in Spring MVC and when would you support multiple response formats?
questions.title: Content Negotiation in Spring MVC — JSON, XML, and Custom Media Types
questions.direct_answer: Content negotiation lets a single endpoint return different formats (JSON, XML, CSV) based on the client's Accept header. Spring MVC's HttpMessageConverter chain selects the converter matching the requested media type. Spring Boot auto-configures JSON support via Jackson; XML requires adding jackson-dataformat-xml to the classpath.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands how the Accept header drives response format selection through HttpMessageConverter.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming @RestController always returns JSON — if an XML converter is on the classpath, clients requesting Accept: application/xml get XML.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three negotiation strategies (Accept header, URL extension, query parameter) and how produces attribute on @RequestMapping locks the format.

sections.title: Your API Silently Changes Format When You Add a Dependency
sections.content:
Most developers assume `@RestController` guarantees JSON responses. It does not. The annotation only tells Spring to write the return value directly to the response body — **the format depends entirely on which `HttpMessageConverter` implementations are registered and what the client asks for.**

Spring Boot auto-configures `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` for JSON because Jackson is on the classpath by default. But the moment you add `jackson-dataformat-xml` — often pulled in transitively by another library — every endpoint starts honoring `Accept: application/xml` requests. No code change, no opt-in, no warning. A client that was getting JSON yesterday gets XML today because someone added a dependency for an unrelated feature.

The mechanism behind this is the **`ContentNegotiationManager`**. When a request arrives, it resolves the client's preferred media type (typically from the `Accept` header), then walks the registered converter chain. The first converter that can serialize the return type into the requested media type wins. If multiple converters match, order matters — and Spring Boot's auto-configured order isn't always what you'd expect.

sections.title: How Spring Selects a Converter — The Three-Step Resolution
Locking Format With produces — Why Implicit Negotiation Is a Production Risk
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Accept` header drives content negotiation by default** — `Accept: application/json` selects `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter`; `Accept: application/xml` selects `Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter` if JAXB is on the classpath.
- **Adding an XML converter changes the default response type** — if `jackson-dataformat-xml` is on the classpath, a request with `Accept: */*` may receive XML instead of JSON; fix with `@RequestMapping(produces = "application/json")`.
- **`@RequestMapping(produces)` filters which requests the handler accepts** — `produces = "application/json"` means the mapping is only invoked for clients that accept JSON; `406 Not Acceptable` if no match.
- **URL extension negotiation is deprecated in Spring 5.3+** — `/orders.json` and `/orders.xml` URL suffixes are disabled by default; prefer Accept header negotiation.
- **`HttpMessageConverter` order matters for `Accept: */*`** — the first converter that supports the return type and `*/*` wins; register converters in priority order in `WebMvcConfigurer.configureMessageConverters()`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Content negotiation is how Spring MVC decides the format of the response — JSON, XML, or something custom — based on what the client declares it can accept.

**How negotiation works**
- Client sends `Accept: application/json` or `Accept: application/xml` in the request header
- Spring walks the registered `HttpMessageConverter` list and finds the first one that can produce the requested media type for the return type
- If no converter matches, Spring returns `406 Not Acceptable`

**Default converters**
- JSON: `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` (from `spring-boot-starter-web`)
- XML: `MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter` (add `jackson-dataformat-xml`) or `Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter`
- Strings, byte arrays, multipart: built-in converters registered automatically

**The `Accept: */*` trap**
- A browser sends `Accept: */*` — it will accept anything
- If XML converter is registered and appears first, browsers may receive XML instead of JSON
- Fix: use `@RequestMapping(produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)` to pin the response type, or register JSON converter first in `configureMessageConverters()`

For APIs that only ever produce JSON, pin `produces = "application/json"` at the controller class level — explicit is better than relying on converter ordering.

sections.title: ResponseEntity Gives You the HTTP Envelope — Most Endpoints Don't Need It
sections.content:
Spring controllers can return objects directly — `return user;` — and Spring wraps them in a 200 OK response with JSON serialization handled automatically. `ResponseEntity` exists for the cases where you need to control the **HTTP envelope itself**: the status code, the headers, or both.

The mistake most developers make is reaching for `ResponseEntity<User>` on every method. A simple GET that returns an object with 200 doesn't benefit from `ResponseEntity` — it adds ceremony without value. The plain return type is cleaner, reads better, and does exactly the same thing.

`ResponseEntity` earns its place in three situations: when you need a **non-200 status code** (201 Created, 204 No Content, 404 Not Found), when you need to set **response headers** (Location, Cache-Control, custom headers), or when the **response varies by condition** (return the object for success, return an error structure for failure). Outside these cases, a plain return type with `@ResponseStatus` is almost always the better choice.

| POST returning 201 + Location header | Can't set Location header | ✅ `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(obj)` |
| DELETE returning 204 No Content | ✅ `@ResponseStatus(NO_CONTENT)` works | Equivalent but verbose |
| Conditional response (200 or 404) | Requires throwing exception | ✅ Return different status per branch |
| Setting Cache-Control or ETag | Can't set headers | ✅ Full header control |
| Error responses | Let `@ControllerAdvice` handle it | ❌ Don't manually build error ResponseEntity |

Key Points
sections.content:
- **`ResponseEntity<T>` gives full control over status code, response headers, and body** — `@ResponseStatus` is a static annotation; `ResponseEntity` allows runtime decisions based on data.
- **`201 Created` must include `Location` header** — `ResponseEntity.created(URI).body(dto)` sets both status and header; omitting the `Location` header violates the HTTP spec for `POST` → create operations.
- **`ResponseEntity<Void>` for `204 No Content`** — `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()`; never return `ResponseEntity<Object>` with null body — the null is ambiguous.
- **`HttpHeaders` builder pattern is fluent** — `ResponseEntity.ok().header("X-Custom-Header", value).body(dto)` chains header additions.
- **Return `ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail>` from exception handlers in Spring Boot 3.x** — produces RFC 7807 compliant error responses with full control over status and body.

- `ResponseEntity.ok(body)` — `200 OK` with body
- `ResponseEntity.created(location).body(dto)` — `201 Created` with `Location` header and body
- `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()` — `204 No Content` with empty body

- The status code depends on runtime logic (created vs existing resource → `201` vs `200`)
- Custom response headers are needed (`Location`, `ETag`, `X-Request-Id`)

**Type safety**
- `ResponseEntity<OrderDto>` communicates the exact body type to the compiler and Springdoc
- `ResponseEntity<Void>` explicitly signals no body — clearer than `ResponseEntity<Object>` with `null`

questions.direct_answer: File upload uses MultipartFile as a controller parameter with @RequestParam. File download uses ResponseEntity<Resource> with appropriate Content-Disposition headers. For large files, streaming with InputStreamResource avoids loading the entire file into memory. Spring Boot's multipart configuration controls max file size and total request size.

sections.title: The Upload Works Until Someone Sends a 500MB File — Then Your JVM Dies
sections.content:
File upload in Spring Boot is straightforward: accept a `MultipartFile` parameter, call `transferTo()`, and you're done. File download is equally simple: return a `Resource` with the right headers. The interview question isn't about making it work — it's about making it work **without crashing in production.**

The default `MultipartFile` implementation buffers the entire file in memory before your controller method even executes. A 500MB upload consumes 500MB of heap. Two concurrent uploads of that size and your JVM runs out of memory. The first thing any production file upload needs is **size limits** — `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` and `spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size` in application properties. These reject oversized uploads at the Tomcat level before Spring even processes the request.

The download side has the same trap in reverse: loading a file into a `byte[]` and returning it works for small files but causes `OutOfMemoryError` when someone downloads a report that grew to 200MB. The fix is **streaming** — `InputStreamResource` or `StreamingResponseBody` write directly to the response output stream without loading the entire file into memory.

sections.title: Upload — MultipartFile With Size Limits and Validation
Download — Why InputStreamResource Prevents the OutOfMemoryError
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`MultipartFile.getInputStream()` does not buffer the entire file in memory by default** — Spring writes parts to a temp directory above `spring.servlet.multipart.file-size-threshold`; access via `getInputStream()` streams from disk.
- **Set `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` and `max-request-size`** — defaults are 1MB; large uploads without limits exhaust heap; set both to a sensible ceiling and enforce at the API gateway too.
- **Stream downloads with `StreamingResponseBody`** — avoid loading the entire file into memory before writing; write chunks to `OutputStream` in a background thread; Tomcat's thread is released while data streams.
- **`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="..."` triggers browser download** — without this header, browsers try to render the file inline; quote the filename and use `filename*=UTF-8''...` for non-ASCII names.
- **S3 pre-signed URLs for large files** — instead of routing large uploads/downloads through the application, generate a pre-signed S3 URL and redirect the client; the app handles only metadata, not bytes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
File upload and download are common requirements with non-obvious memory management concerns. The wrong approach loads entire files into JVM heap — a denial-of-service risk with large files.

**Upload**
- Accept `MultipartFile` in the controller: `@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file`
- `file.getInputStream()` streams the upload content; for small files `file.getBytes()` reads all bytes into memory — be careful with the `max-file-size` limit
- Set `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size=50MB` and `max-request-size=55MB` in `application.properties`; also configure at the API gateway or load balancer

**Download**
- Return `ResponseEntity<Resource>` with `InputStreamResource` wrapping a file input stream — Spring streams to the client
- Or return `StreamingResponseBody` for full control over chunked writing; runs in a separate thread, releasing the Tomcat worker thread
- Always set `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="filename.pdf"` and `Content-Type` headers

**S3 pre-signed URLs — the production pattern for large files**
- Application generates a pre-signed URL with a short TTL (5-15 minutes)
- Client uploads directly to S3 or downloads directly from S3 — application never handles the bytes
- Eliminates egress bandwidth cost on the application tier and scales to any file size

questions.question: What is HATEOAS and when does it actually add value in a Spring Boot REST API?
questions.title: HATEOAS — Hypermedia-Driven REST APIs with Spring HATEOAS
questions.direct_answer: HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) means API responses include links to related resources and available actions. Spring HATEOAS provides RepresentationModel and WebMvcLinkBuilder to add links programmatically. It adds value when API consumers shouldn't hardcode URLs or when available actions depend on resource state, but adds overhead for internal APIs with tightly coupled clients.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands HATEOAS beyond the definition and can evaluate when it's worth the complexity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Either dismissing HATEOAS entirely or claiming it's required for REST — the right answer evaluates trade-offs.

sections.title: Links in Responses Sound Academic Until Your API Has State-Dependent Actions
sections.content:
HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) means the API response includes links telling the client what it can do next. An order response doesn't just contain order data — it includes links to cancel, pay, or ship, depending on the order's current state. The client doesn't hardcode URLs or guess which actions are valid; it follows the links the server provides.

Most developers either dismiss HATEOAS as ivory-tower REST theory or claim it's required for any "real" REST API. Both positions miss the point. HATEOAS adds genuine value in exactly two situations: when **actions depend on state** (an order can only be cancelled before it ships) and when **external consumers need to navigate your API without hardcoding paths** (third-party integrations, public APIs). For an internal service-to-service API where both sides are controlled by the same team, HATEOAS adds complexity without benefit.

This is Richardson Maturity Level 3 — the highest level of REST maturity. Level 0 is "one URL, POST everything." Level 1 introduces resources. Level 2 adds proper HTTP methods. Level 3 adds hypermedia links. Most production APIs stop at Level 2 because Level 3's value is situational, not universal.

sections.title: How Spring HATEOAS Builds Links — WebMvcLinkBuilder In Practice
When HATEOAS Is Worth the Complexity — And When It Isn't
sections.content:
**Use HATEOAS when:** your API has state machines (orders, approvals, workflows) where available actions change based on current state; your API is consumed by external teams who shouldn't hardcode your URL structure; you need to evolve API paths without breaking clients.

**Skip HATEOAS when:** both client and server are controlled by the same team and deployed together; your API is simple CRUD with no state-dependent actions; you're building a backend-for-frontend (BFF) where the frontend team already knows every endpoint.

The overhead is real: every response carries extra link data, your assemblers add code, and clients need to understand link relations. For internal microservices communicating over gRPC or simple REST, this overhead buys nothing. For a public API with dozens of external integrators, it prevents the alternative — which is every integrator hardcoding your URLs and breaking when you restructure.

One practical middle ground: use **link relations in error responses** even if you don't do full HATEOAS. When a 403 response includes a link to the authentication endpoint, or a 404 includes a link to search — that's hypermedia adding value without the full overhead of wrapping every response in `EntityModel`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HATEOAS is REST Level 3 — clients navigate the API via links, not hardcoded URIs** — responses include `_links` with `href` values for related actions; clients follow links rather than constructing URLs.
- **Spring HATEOAS `EntityModel<T>` wraps a DTO with links** — `EntityModel.of(dto, linkTo(methodOn(OrderController.class).getOrder(id)).withSelfRel())`.
- **`WebMvcLinkBuilder.linkTo(methodOn(...))` builds type-safe links** — refactoring the controller method signature or URL updates the link automatically; string-based URI building breaks silently.
- **HAL (Hypertext Application Language) is the most common HATEOAS format** — `_links` object with `self`, `next`, `prev`, and action links; Spring HATEOAS produces HAL by default.
- **HATEOAS adoption is limited in practice** — Level 2 (HTTP verbs + status codes) is the pragmatic target for most teams; HATEOAS adds complexity without clear benefit unless clients are third-party and need to discover endpoints.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HATEOAS — Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State — is the Level 3 REST constraint where API responses include links to related resources and available actions. Clients navigate the API by following links rather than constructing URLs from documentation.

**Why it matters**
- A client fetching `/orders/123` receives links to `cancel`, `ship`, `payment` based on the order's current state
- The server controls which actions are available — a cancelled order does not include a `cancel` link
- Clients never hardcode URLs; URI changes on the server side do not break clients

**Spring HATEOAS implementation**
- `EntityModel.of(orderDto)` wraps a DTO
- `.add(linkTo(methodOn(OrderController.class).getOrder(id)).withSelfRel())` adds a `self` link using the controller method signature — type-safe, refactoring-safe
- `CollectionModel<EntityModel<OrderDto>>` wraps a collection with collection-level links (`self`, `next`, `prev` for pagination)

**HAL format**
- Spring HATEOAS produces HAL (Hypertext Application Language) by default: `{"id": 123, "_links": {"self": {"href": "/orders/123"}, "cancel": {"href": "/orders/123/cancel"}}}`

In practice: most teams stop at Richardson Level 2. HATEOAS is worth implementing for public APIs where third-party clients need to discover endpoints, or for APIs where workflow state determines available actions.

questions.direct_answer: Exposing JPA entities directly in API responses couples your database schema to your API contract, leaks internal fields (like password hashes), triggers lazy loading exceptions, and makes API evolution impossible without database migration. DTOs create a boundary between internal representation and external contract, letting each evolve independently.

sections.title: Exposing JPA Entities Directly Is a Ticking Time Bomb — Here's What Breaks
sections.content:
Returning a JPA entity from a controller feels efficient — one class serves the database, the API, and the business logic. In practice, it creates three problems that get worse as the application grows.

**Problem one: `LazyInitializationException`.** JPA loads `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` relationships lazily by default. When Jackson tries to serialize the entity outside the persistence context (which is closed by the time the response is written), it triggers a `LazyInitializationException`. Developers work around this with `FetchType.EAGER` or `@Transactional` on the controller — both are worse than the original problem. Eager loading pulls the entire object graph on every query. `@Transactional` on the controller keeps the database connection open during serialization, wasting connection pool resources.

**Problem two: API coupling.** Every database schema change — renaming a column, adding a field, restructuring a relationship — changes the API response. Clients break on every migration. With DTOs, the API contract and the database schema evolve independently.

**Problem three: security leaks.** Entities often contain fields that should never reach the client — password hashes, internal IDs, audit timestamps, soft-delete flags. `@JsonIgnore` works until someone forgets it on a new field.

sections.title: Request DTOs vs Response DTOs — Why They Should Be Different Classes
The Mapping Layer — Where Conversion Lives Without Polluting Business Logic
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never expose entities directly in REST responses** — exposing JPA entities as response bodies leaks database column names, triggers lazy loading in the serializer, and couples your API contract to your database schema.
- **Separate request DTOs from response DTOs** — `CreateOrderRequest` (what comes in) and `OrderResponse` (what goes out) are different shapes; combining them forces unnecessary fields or awkward nullability.
- **MapStruct generates compile-time DTO mappers with zero reflection** — `@Mapper` interface + method signatures; MapStruct generates the implementation; type-safe, IDE-navigable, no runtime cost.
- **Record classes (Java 16+) are ideal for immutable response DTOs** — `record OrderResponse(Long id, String status, BigDecimal total) {}` — no boilerplate, immutable, serializes correctly with Jackson.
- **Validate on the request DTO, not the entity** — Bean Validation annotations belong on `CreateOrderRequest`; the entity should receive only already-validated data from the service layer.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) are the boundary between your HTTP layer and your domain/persistence layer. Skipping them is a shortcut that creates API coupling to database schemas and security vulnerabilities.

**Why not expose entities directly**
- `@JsonIgnore` and `@JsonProperty` on entity fields create maintenance overhead as the schema evolves
- Bidirectional `@OneToMany` relationships cause infinite recursion during JSON serialization
- Lazy-loaded fields trigger additional SQL queries inside the Jackson serializer — N+1 inside the serializer
- API consumers see internal field names and column-level details that break when you refactor the database

**Request vs response DTOs**
- Request DTO: fields needed to perform the operation, with validation annotations; fields the client is not allowed to set (like `createdAt`) are absent
- Response DTO: fields the client needs to see, potentially aggregated from multiple entities, with no persistence metadata

**Mapping options**
- MapStruct: annotation processor generates compile-time implementation; zero reflection; method signature = mapping contract
- ModelMapper: runtime reflection; simpler setup; harder to debug; slower
- Manual mapping: explicit but verbose; acceptable for small projects

Java records (`record OrderResponse(Long id, String status) {}`) are the cleanest response DTO — immutable, compact, and Jackson-serializable without configuration.

questions.direct_answer: Each HTTP method maps to a CRUD operation with specific semantics: GET retrieves (safe, idempotent, cacheable), POST creates (not idempotent), PUT replaces entirely (idempotent), PATCH modifies partially (idempotency depends on operation), DELETE removes (idempotent). Using methods correctly enables caching, safe retries, and clear API semantics.

sections.title: HTTP Methods Are Not CRUD Labels — They're Contracts With Infrastructure
sections.content:
Most developers learn HTTP methods as CRUD shortcuts: GET = read, POST = create, PUT = update, DELETE = delete. This mental model works for simple APIs but misses the properties that actually matter: **safety** and **idempotency**. These properties aren't just theoretical — they determine how proxies cache responses, whether load balancers can retry failed requests, and how API gateways handle traffic.

A **safe** method doesn't modify server state. GET and HEAD are safe — calling them has no side effects. This is why browsers pre-fetch links, search engines crawl your URLs, and CDNs cache GET responses. If your GET endpoint modifies data (a common anti-pattern), caches serve stale data and crawlers trigger unintended writes.

An **idempotent** method produces the same result regardless of how many times it's called. GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent. POST is not. This is why load balancers can safely retry a failed PUT — sending it twice doesn't create two resources. Retrying a failed POST, however, might create a duplicate. Understanding this distinction is the difference between designing APIs that work reliably with infrastructure and ones that fight it.

sections.title: Method Properties — What Infrastructure Assumes About Each Method
sections.content:
| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Body | Typical Use | Infrastructure Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | ✅ | ✅ | No | Retrieve resource | Cached by CDNs and proxies |
| POST | ❌ | ❌ | Yes | Create resource, trigger action | Never cached, never retried automatically |
| PUT | ❌ | ✅ | Yes | Replace entire resource | Safe to retry on failure |
| PATCH | ❌ | Depends | Yes | Partial update | Not guaranteed idempotent |
| DELETE | ❌ | ✅ | Optional | Remove resource | Safe to retry on failure |
| HEAD | ✅ | ✅ | No | Check resource existence | Same as GET without body |

The "Infrastructure Behavior" column is why method choice matters beyond semantics. Using POST for an idempotent operation means your load balancer won't retry it on failure — you lose automatic resilience that PUT and DELETE get for free.

sections.title: PUT vs PATCH vs POST — The Decision That Reveals Your Understanding
sections.content:
The most common follow-up: "when do you use PUT vs PATCH?" The answer reveals whether you've thought about partial updates.

**PUT replaces the entire resource.** If you PUT a user with only `name` and `email`, every other field becomes null (or its default). This is the contract — the request body IS the new state. PUT is idempotent because sending the same request twice produces the same result.

**PATCH modifies specific fields.** Only the fields in the request body change; everything else stays. PATCH is NOT inherently idempotent — a PATCH that says "increment counter by 1" gives a different result each time. A PATCH that says "set name to John" is idempotent. The idempotency depends on the operation, not the method.

**POST is the catch-all.** It creates resources, triggers actions, processes payments — anything that doesn't fit the other methods. The key constraint: POST is not idempotent and not safe. Using POST for everything ("POST tunneling") throws away the guarantees that GET, PUT, and DELETE give you. Caches don't work, retries aren't safe, and API documentation loses clarity.

In Spring MVC, the mapping is explicit: `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping`, `@DeleteMapping`. Using the correct annotation isn't just convention — it generates accurate OpenAPI documentation and enables Spring Security's method-level security to work correctly.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GET and HEAD are safe and idempotent; DELETE and PUT are idempotent but not safe** — safe = no side effects; idempotent = same state result on repeat; POST is neither.
- **GET must not have a request body** — some frameworks allow it, but HTTP/1.1 semantics say GET body has no defined meaning; use query parameters or POST for complex query criteria.
- **PUT sends the full resource representation; PATCH sends a partial update** — a PUT with a partial body nulls out missing fields; PATCH applies only what is present.
- **DELETE returning `404` on the second call is still idempotent** — server state (resource absent) is the same; only the response code differs.
- **OPTIONS is the preflight method for CORS** — browsers send `OPTIONS` before cross-origin non-simple requests; the server must respond with allowed methods and origins or the actual request is blocked.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HTTP methods are not just routing conventions — they carry semantic contracts about idempotency, safety, and caching that clients, proxies, and CDNs rely on.

**The four dimensions**
- **Safe** — no server-side state change: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
- **Idempotent** — same server state on repeated calls: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE
- **Cacheable** — responses may be cached: GET, HEAD (by default), POST with explicit headers
- **Request body allowed** — semantic convention: POST, PUT, PATCH (yes); GET, DELETE (technically allowed but semantically undefined)

**Decision guide**
- Retrieve a resource or collection → GET
- Create a new resource (server assigns ID) → POST
- Replace a resource completely (client knows ID) → PUT
- Partially modify a resource → PATCH
- Remove a resource → DELETE
- Discover available methods (CORS preflight) → OPTIONS

**Common mistakes**
- POST for everything: loses idempotency and cacheability signals for clients and CDNs
- GET with a request body for complex search: use POST to `/orders/search` with a request body for complex filter criteria — GET body is semantically undefined
- DELETE that is not idempotent: throwing `404` on the second call is fine; the state (resource gone) is the same
